the angel of the Lord in a dream
the angel of the Lord said

examples.everyday: My grandmother used to say the angel of the Lord was keeping watch over our house.
examples.professional: In the sermon outline, I will contrast the angel of the Lord in Genesis with the later messengers in Luke.
examples.analytical: In several Old Testament passages the angel of the Lord shifts into speaking in the first person as God, which has led interpreters to ask whether this messenger is God in a form of appearance.

nuance.analogy: Like an ambassador who speaks so fully for the king that people address the ambassador as if the king were present.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew mal'akh YHWH, where mal'akh means messenger and YHWH is God's covenant name.
common_mistakes: Treating it as a random angel; the phrase refers to a specific figure in certain Old Testament narratives.
Pronouncing 'of the' as 'off the' in careful speech; in normal American speech it is 'uhv thuh'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew phrase is mal'akh YHWH, meaning messenger of the LORD. Genesis 16:7-13 describes the angel of the Lord speaking to Hagar, and she then names God in response. Exodus 3:2-6 describes the angel of the Lord appearing in a flame from a bush, where the voice speaks as God. Judges 6:11-22 describes the angel of the Lord appearing to Gideon and speaking with divine authority.

senses.definition: One who creates an animation or cartoon; a cartoonist.
senses.example: In recent years, animators using computer rendering have largely superseded artists working by hand.

senses.definition: One who animates something; one who brings something to life or the appearance of life.
senses.example: The android turned to gaze at its animator.

core.definition: A person who creates animated films, cartoons, or computer graphics by drawing or building images that appear to move.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and pronounce the last syllable as a reduced 'ter' with a clear American r. Avoid adding an extra syllable at the end.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes a creative professional whose work brings characters and objects to life.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'animator' for people who work in film studios, game studios, or advertising, creating motion through drawing, 3D modeling, or software. It is not usually a word for a cartoonist, who draws comics or editorial cartoons. In casual talk, people might say 'he works in animation' or 'she does cartoons for a living.'

distinctions.note: A cartoonist draws comics or cartoons, often as still images; an animator makes drawings or models move over time.
An illustrator creates still pictures for books, articles, or advertisements; an animator creates sequences of motion.

collocations: an animator for a game studio

examples.everyday: My cousin is an animator who works on video games, so she is always busy this time of year.
examples.professional: We need a senior animator on the team to finish the character rigging for the product demo.
examples.analytical: The animator's work reveals how a character's gestures can communicate an inner life that the script does not state directly.

nuance.analogy: An animator is like a puppeteer working one frame at a time, giving each small movement a reason to happen.
nuance.etymology: From 'animate' plus the agent suffix '-or,' from Latin 'animare,' to give life to.
common_mistakes: Using 'animator' to mean a cartoonist who draws only still comics.
Pronouncing the last syllable as 'tor' with a strong vowel instead of a reduced 'ter.'

senses.definition: Not isochronous.

core.definition: Not isochronous; occurring at unequal time intervals, or taking unequal times to complete repeated cycles.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SOK, the same syllable as in isochronous. The an- prefix is light and the middle vowel is a long eye sound, and many learners wrongly stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a purely descriptive technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in physics, signal processing, music theory and rhythm research to describe events or pulses that do not recur at equal intervals. Outside technical writing, Americans say uneven or irregular instead. The word fits a lab report or methods section, not casual talk.

distinctions.note: Asynchronous means not happening at the same time or not coordinated in time, while anisochronous specifically means the intervals between repeated events are unequal.
Irregular is everyday and broad, covering any departure from a pattern; anisochronous is precise and refers only to the timing of intervals.

examples.professional: The sensor logs readings at anisochronous intervals, so we need to resample the data before we fit the model.
examples.analytical: A rhythm whose beats fall at anisochronous intervals resists the simple periodic models that work well for a metronome.

nuance.analogy: Like a drummer who keeps forgetting to come back on the beat, so the gaps between hits keep changing.
nuance.etymology: From Greek an- (not) plus isochronous, from isos (equal) and chronos (time).
common_mistakes: Confusing it with asynchronous, which describes events not occurring together rather than unequal time spacing.
Putting the stress on the first syllable instead of SOK in the middle of the word.

senses.definition: American and Oxford British spelling of annualize.

core.definition: To convert a figure or rate, such as revenue or a monthly cost, into the equivalent amount for a full year.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on AN, the first syllable, and the last syllable sounds like eyes, not iz. Keep the middle glide quick, so the word has three clear parts.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical, used in business and finance without emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use annualize in finance, business reports, and data analysis, as in annualized revenue or annualized return. The American spelling is annualize, while the British spelling is annualise. In casual speech people say convert to a yearly amount.

distinctions.note: Annual is an adjective meaning yearly; annualize is the verb for converting a shorter figure into a yearly one.
Prorate divides a charge across a partial period; annualize extends a partial period's figure to a full year.

examples.everyday: My bank statement shows monthly interest, but I like to annualize it so I can compare savings accounts.
examples.professional: Let's annualize the three-month churn figure so we can compare it with last year's report.
examples.analytical: Annualizing short-term growth rates can exaggerate trends, since a few strong weeks may not hold across a full year.

nuance.analogy: Like turning a weekly grocery total into a yearly budget, keeping the same pattern but scaling it up.
nuance.etymology: From annual, from Latin annualis, from annus 'year'.
common_mistakes: Spelling it annualise, which is British; American usage is annualize.
Confusing the verb annualize with the adjective annual; use annual before a noun, as in annual report.

senses.definition: Before (in time).
senses.example: The historian noted that the treaty was signed anteriorly to the revolution, which changed the timeline.

senses.definition: In front (in position).
Towards the anterior.

core.definition: Toward or at the front part of something, especially the front of the body.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on TEER, the second syllable. The -ior ending is a reduced 'ee-er' sound, and the final -ly is clear and light.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; common in medicine, anatomy and engineering descriptions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'anteriorly' mostly in medicine, anatomy and technical writing, while in everyday speech they say 'in front' or 'toward the front.' For time, use 'earlier' or 'before' rather than this word. Doctors often say 'anteriorly' when describing the location of pain or a structure.

distinctions.note: Anterior is an adjective for the front part, while anteriorly is an adverb describing the direction or location of an action.
Frontally is used for approach or direction from the front, while anteriorly describes a position relative to the front of an anatomical structure.

examples.everyday: My doctor said the pain is mostly anteriorly, toward the front of my knee.
examples.professional: The model places the sensor anteriorly on the robot's chassis to reduce occlusion from the arm.
examples.analytical: In the diagram, the second vertebra shifts anteriorly, so the curve of the spine tilts forward.

nuance.analogy: Like the headlights at the front of a car, while the taillights sit at the back.
nuance.etymology: From Latin anterior, 'more forward,' plus the adverbial suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using 'anteriorly' for time, where 'earlier' or 'before' is correct.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'an-tee-ree-OR-lee.'

senses.definition: That reduces anxiety; tranquilizing.
A drug prescribed for the treatment of symptoms of anxiety.
senses.example: The psychiatrist prescribed a mild anxiolytic to help him sleep during the stressful months.

core.definition: Reducing anxiety; or a drug that reduces anxiety, sometimes called an anti-anxiety medication.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the -LIT- syllable, and the first syllable starts with 'ang', not 'ax'. The final -ic is a short 'ik' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise clinical term without emotional coloring.
nuance.usage_note: This is mainly a medical or pharmacy term. Ordinary Americans say 'anti-anxiety medication' or 'anxiety medicine', and doctors may name the specific drug class instead. In casual talk, 'anxiolytic' sounds overly clinical, so use it in medical writing or when discussing drug classes.

distinctions.note: A sedative makes you drowsy or calm, often at higher doses, while an anxiolytic specifically targets anxiety, though many drugs do both.
An antidepressant treats depression, though some are also used for anxiety, while anxiolytics are often used for short-term relief of anxiety.
Tranquilizer is an older, broader term for drugs that calm, while anxiolytic is the precise medical term.

examples.everyday: My doctor said the new pill is an anxiolytic, but it might make me drowsy.
examples.professional: The pharmacist reviewed the anxiolytic dosage with the patient before the surgery.
examples.analytical: The study tested whether the anxiolytic effect of the compound can be separated from its sedative action.

nuance.analogy: An anxiolytic is like a dimmer switch for worry, turning down the intensity of anxiety.
nuance.etymology: From anxiety plus Greek lytikos, able to loosen, from lyein meaning to loosen.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a long a as 'ax-ee-OH-lit-ik'; the stress is on LIT and the first syllable has a nasal 'ang'.
Using it as a casual word for anything calming; it refers to drugs or anxiety-reducing effects.

senses.definition: That does not recur periodically.
senses.example: aperiodic tiling

senses.definition: For which any return to it may occur at irregular times; not periodic.
senses.example: The engineer noticed that the sensor produced aperiodic spikes that arrived at irregular intervals.

senses.definition: That does not have a periodic vibration.
senses.example: The shock absorber produced an aperiodic vibration that died away without any oscillation.

core.definition: Not repeating at regular intervals; having no fixed period or cycle, as with a signal, sequence, or motion.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on AH, the 'od' syllable, with a light secondary stress on 'ay'. The middle syllables reduce, so 'per' sounds like 'pir' and 'i' like 'ee' but very short.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'aperiodic' in mathematics, physics, engineering, and data analysis to describe patterns that do not repeat on a schedule. Outside technical work, people more often say 'irregular' or 'random'. Be careful: 'aperiodic' says nothing about randomness, only about the absence of a repeating cycle.

distinctions.note: In many fields the two mean the same, but aperiodic is more common in signal processing, while nonperiodic appears more broadly.
Random means unpredictable in value or timing, while aperiodic only means it never repeats in a regular cycle; a random signal is aperiodic, but not all aperiodic signals are random.
Irregular is a general word for uneven or inconsistent, while aperiodic is a precise technical term about repetition.

examples.everyday: The rain on the tin roof was aperiodic, with no steady rhythm at all.
examples.professional: The sensor data showed aperiodic spikes, so the periodicity test failed and we switched to an anomaly detection model.
examples.analytical: An aperiodic signal does not repeat, so its frequency content must be described by a continuous spectrum rather than discrete harmonics.

nuance.analogy: Like a song that never returns to its chorus: it moves forward without a pattern that comes back on a schedule.
nuance.etymology: From Greek a- 'not' and periodic, from Greek periodikos 'recurring at intervals'.
common_mistakes: Using 'aperiodic' to mean 'random' in everyday speech, when the word only describes the lack of a repeating cycle.
Stressing the first syllable, which makes the word sound unnatural in American technical speech.

senses.definition: Incontrovertible; demonstrably true or certain.
Being a style of argument in which a person presents their reasoning as categorically true, even if it is not necessarily so.
senses.example: Don’t be so apodictic! You haven’t considered several facets of the question.

senses.definition: Absolute and without explanation, as in a command from God like "Thou shalt not kill!"
senses.example: The rabbi taught that the commandment Thou shalt not kill is apodictic, needing no justification.

core.definition: Logically certain and proven beyond doubt by reasoning, so that it must be true rather than merely probable.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the third syllable, DIK. Keep the first vowel as the short 'a' in 'cat', and do not reduce the middle syllable too much, or it will blur into 'ap-DIK'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when describing proof or knowledge. It can sound arrogant when applied to someone's personal opinions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in philosophy, logic, mathematics and academic writing, especially when discussing Kant. In everyday speech it sounds like a seminar term, and if you use it in casual talk people may smile. Instead, say 'airtight', 'indisputable' or 'there's no way around it'. The related spelling 'apodeictic' is also accepted in American academic writing.

distinctions.note: Axiomatic describes something accepted as a self-evident starting point, while apodictic describes a conclusion that follows with necessity from reasoning.
Dogmatic means insisting on a view without adequate evidence, which is often criticized; apodictic means the claim is actually logically certain.
A contingent truth could have been otherwise, while an apodictic truth is necessary and could not be false.

examples.everyday: You say that like it's apodictic truth, but you read it on one blog post last week.
examples.professional: The model only gives apodictic guarantees if the samples are independent, so the report should state that assumption clearly.
examples.analytical: Kant held that mathematical propositions are apodictic, because their necessity is grasped through reason rather than learned from experience.

nuance.analogy: Like a proof that two plus two equals four: you don't need to check examples, because the reasoning settles the matter completely.
nuance.etymology: From Greek apodeiktikos, 'capable of demonstration', from apodeiknynai, 'to show forth, demonstrate'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'apoplectic', which means furiously angry, and the two words sound somewhat alike.
Using it for a strong opinion. It means logically certain, not merely confident or forceful.

apodictic.etymology: From the Latin *apodīcticus* (“proving clearly”, “demonstrative”), from the Ancient Greek *ἀποδεικτικός* (“affording proof”, “demonstrative”), from *ἀποδείκνυμι* (“to demonstrate”).

senses.definition: Having the character of apology; regretfully excusing.
senses.example: His tone was apologetic as he explained what had happened.

senses.definition: (dated) Defending by words or arguments; said or written in defense.
senses.example: Her apologetic essay defended the treaty against critics who had called it a betrayal.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: A defensive method of argument.
senses.example: Her course on modern apologetic taught us how to answer skeptics with reasoned argument.

core.definition: Showing or expressing regret for having caused trouble, hurt, or inconvenience, and asking for forgiveness.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on JEH, the third syllable, with a lighter secondary stress on pah. The first and third syllables use reduced vowels, and the final -tic sounds like 'tik,' not 'teek.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, depending on context. It describes a sincere, polite sorrow, but it can imply the speaker is weak or overly submissive if used too much.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use apologetic in everyday speech and in workplace writing, often with 'about' or 'for,' as in 'She was apologetic about the delay.' Saying 'I'm so sorry' is more common in conversation, while apologetic describes a person's tone or manner. A natural reply to someone who seems apologetic is 'No worries' or 'It's fine.'

distinctions.note: Sorry is the everyday word people say directly, while apologetic describes someone's manner or tone of regret.
Remorseful implies deep guilt about a serious wrong, while apologetic usually suggests a lighter, polite regret over a smaller mistake.

examples.everyday: The waiter brought our order late, but he was so apologetic that we didn't mind at all.
examples.professional: Our vendor sent an apologetic email after the server outage, and they offered a credit on next month's invoice.
examples.analytical: The author's tone is apologetic, yet the argument it defends is quite assertive, which creates an interesting tension in the essay.

nuance.analogy: An apologetic person is like someone who steps back and says 'Oops, sorry, after you' when they bump into you, showing they noticed the trouble they caused.
nuance.etymology: From Greek apologia, meaning a defense or speech in defense, through Latin and Old French, with the sense of regret added in later English use.
common_mistakes: Using apologetic as a noun when the noun form is apology.
Saying 'apologetic for' the mistake; the usual pattern is 'apologetic about' or 'apologetic for,' but 'apologetic about' is more common in everyday American speech.

apologetic.etymology: From French *apologétique*, from Latin *apologēticus*, from Ancient Greek *ἀπολογητικός* (“of or suitable for defense”), from *ἀπολογέομαι* (“to speak in defense of”); see more at.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to an appellative noun or common noun.
senses.example: (Can we add an example for this sense?)

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to ascribing names.
senses.example: (Can we add an example for this sense?)

senses.definition: A common noun.
An epithet.
senses.example: (Can we add an example for this sense? (all senses))

core.definition: A common noun, or a name or title that identifies a class of people or things rather than one specific individual.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PEL. The last syllables are weak, so say 'uh-tiv' with a short vowel, not 'uh-TIVE' with a long one.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise grammar and linguistics term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use appellative in daily life; in school and most writing they say 'common noun' for the same idea. The word appears in linguistics, philosophy, and classical scholarship, especially when contrasting it with proper noun. As an adjective, appellative describes something that names or titles a class of things.

distinctions.note: A proper noun names a specific person, place, or thing, while an appellative names a general class, such as 'teacher' or 'river'.
An appellation is a formal name or title, while an appellative is a common noun or a descriptive name for a class.

examples.everyday: My daughter's grammar homework asked whether teacher is an appellative or a proper noun.
examples.professional: In our data dictionary, customer is an appellative label, so we need to standardize how it is defined.
examples.analytical: Scholastic logicians debated whether words used of God are appellative or proper, a question about how names refer to things.

nuance.analogy: Like a job title on a name tag: it tells you what category someone belongs to, not who they are.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin appellativus, from Latin appellare, to call or name.
common_mistakes: Confusing appellative (grammar, naming) with appellate (court appeals), which sound similar but have different meanings.
Using appellative as a simple synonym for name, when it really refers to a common noun or descriptive class name.

appellative.etymology: From the Late Latin *appellātīvus*, from the stem, with the adjectival suffix *-īvus*.

senses.definition: A person who is appointed.
senses.example: The ambassador is a political appointee, not a career diplomat.

core.definition: A person chosen for a job or position by someone in authority, such as a president, governor or board, rather than by voters.

pronunciation.tip: Put the main stress on the last syllable, TEE, and keep the first syllable light: uh-poyn-TEE, not POY-nee. The final -ee is a long e.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it names a role without judging the person's qualifications, though news coverage may add criticism or praise.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use appointee mainly in news and government contexts, often in phrases like 'a political appointee' or 'a presidential appointee'. The word can hint at favoritism when people add political to it. In casual talk you would say 'she got the job through the governor' or 'she's the mayor's pick' instead. It is common in writing and formal speech.

distinctions.note: A nominee has been proposed but may not yet be confirmed; an appointee already holds the position.
Employee is the general word for anyone working for a company; appointee specifically means someone selected by an authority for a post.

examples.everyday: My cousin is a state appointee, so she got the job through the governor's office.
examples.professional: The new director is a political appointee, so we should expect some changes in priorities.
examples.analytical: Each appointee serves at the pleasure of the president, which raises questions about independence in agency decisions.

nuance.analogy: An appointee is like a substitute teacher picked by the principal: they hold the role because someone with authority chose them.
nuance.etymology: From appoint, from Old French apointer, plus the suffix -ee for the person who receives an action.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (POY-nee) instead of the last syllable, TEE.
Confusing appointee with nominee; a nominee has not yet been confirmed.

senses.definition: A natural ability to acquire knowledge or skill.
senses.example: She showed an early aptitude for mathematics.

senses.definition: The condition of being suitable.

core.definition: A natural talent or ability to learn a particular skill or subject.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the first syllable, AP, and the second part, -tude, gets a secondary stress that sounds like 'tood' or 'tyood'. Do not pronounce the 'p' and 't' as separate sounds with a vowel between them.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests potential and natural promise, so people usually describe someone's aptitude in praise or neutrally.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use aptitude in schools, job interviews, and career discussions, such as 'She has an aptitude for languages' or 'aptitude test'. In casual speech, people often say 'she's a natural' or 'he's good at it'. Used about yourself, it sounds a bit formal but is fine in interviews.

distinctions.note: Ability is the current capacity to do something. Aptitude is the natural potential to learn it, often before any training.
Talent suggests an exceptional gift, while aptitude can be moderate and still useful.
Skill is acquired through practice. Aptitude is the underlying natural readiness that makes learning the skill easier.

examples.everyday: My daughter has a real aptitude for drawing, so we signed her up for art class.
examples.professional: The hiring manager said the candidate showed a strong aptitude for data analysis during the technical screen.
examples.analytical: Plato would distinguish innate aptitude from acquired knowledge, asking which one truly makes a person a philosopher.

nuance.analogy: Like a seed that already holds the shape of a particular tree, ready to grow well with the right care.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin aptitudo 'fitness, suitability', from Latin aptus 'fitted, suitable'.
common_mistakes: Confusing aptitude with attitude, which means outlook or feelings.
Saying aptitude to instead of aptitude for.
Stressing the wrong syllable, for example AP-ti-TUDE with the last syllable too strong.
patterns: [C, U] (an) aptitude for sth/for doing sth

aptitude.etymology: From Middle French *aptitude*, from Medieval Latin *aptitudo*, from Latin *aptus* (“apt, fit”).

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to an archive or archiving.
Of a material: having a quality suited to the conservational needs of archiving.
senses.example: archival boxes archival paper

senses.definition: The practice of storing items in an archive; archiving; an instance of this.
senses.example: Our nightly computer backups include the archival of old e-mail messages.

core.definition: Relating to archives, or preserved for long-term keeping as historical records and documents.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on KY, the second syllable, and the first syllable is light. Do not add a separate ee sound such as ar-chee-val, and the final -al is reduced to a short vul.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It suggests permanence, care, and historical value, and it often describes materials built to last.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use archival in academic research, libraries, museums, and records management, as in archival research or archival footage. The noun archival, meaning the practice of archiving, is much less common than the adjective. In casual talk people often say old or saved instead.

distinctions.note: Archive is the noun for the collection or place, while archival is the adjective describing things related to that collection.
Historical refers to the past in general, while archival specifically means preserved in or drawn from records kept for long-term use.

examples.everyday: The local museum has some archival photos of the old train station, and they are wonderful to look at.
examples.professional: We need archival-quality storage for the 2010 project files, so they will not degrade over the next decade.
examples.analytical: The historian built her argument on archival research rather than on secondary summaries of the same events.

nuance.analogy: Think of a time capsule sealed carefully for future generations: everything inside is chosen and preserved to last.
nuance.etymology: From archive, from Latin archivum, from Greek archeion meaning public records or office.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as AR-ki-vul.
Using archival as a verb, when the verb is archive.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to virtue or excellence.

core.definition: Relating to virtue or moral excellence, especially in philosophy, where it describes ethics based on character rather than rules.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the TAY syllable, and the first syllable sounds like 'air'. Don't stress the first syllable or pronounce the final -aic as 'ay-sik'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and neutral. It praises excellence in character, but it is a technical term used in philosophical discussion, not everyday talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet this word in philosophy classes, ethics papers and discussions of virtue ethics. It describes a view that asks what kind of person you are becoming, as opposed to what rules you must follow. In casual conversation, people would more likely say 'virtue-based' or 'character-based'.

distinctions.note: Deontic describes duties and what is required or forbidden, while aretaic describes the excellences of character a person should develop.
Teleological refers to goals or ends of action, while aretaic focuses on the virtues a person possesses regardless of outcomes.

examples.everyday: Our book club argued about whether the hero was good or just lucky, and someone brought up the aretaic side of it.
examples.professional: Our ethics seminar slides compare the deontic framework with an aretaic approach to character.
examples.analytical: An aretaic account of the good life begins with the excellences of character rather than with rules for action.

nuance.analogy: If deontic ethics is the rulebook, aretaic ethics is the coach who asks what kind of player you are becoming.
nuance.etymology: From Greek aretē, meaning excellence or virtue.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable instead of the TAY syllable.
Confusing it with archaic or arcane, which have different meanings and pronunciations.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word arete (aretē), meaning excellence or virtue, appears in the New Testament. The RSV renders it 'virtue' in 2 Peter 1:5, where believers are urged to add virtue to their faith, and 'excellence' in Philippians 4:8, where Paul asks readers to think about whatever has moral excellence. Scripture thus uses the word for moral goodness that grows from faith and is directed toward God.

senses.definition: As can be supported or proven by sound logical deduction, evidence, and precedent, but without absolute certainty.
senses.example: The 2008 financial crisis was arguably the worst economic event since the Great Depression.

core.definition: Used to say that something can be supported by good reasons, though it is not certain or universally agreed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the middle 'gyoo' flow smoothly. The final '-ly' is a light 'lee', so the word has four syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and hedged. It makes a strong opinion sound measured and reasonable.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'arguably' before superlatives, as in 'arguably the best', to share an opinion without sounding absolute. It is common in reviews, sports talk and business meetings. A natural reply is 'I'd agree' or 'Hard to argue with that'.

distinctions.note: Probably expresses likelihood, while arguably says there is a good case for the claim even though others may disagree.
Possibly only means something could be true, while arguably suggests the claim is well supported.

examples.everyday: That's arguably the best burger in town, so let's go there.
examples.professional: Pricing is arguably our biggest lever for retention this quarter, so let's test it first.
examples.analytical: Kant's ethics is arguably more systematic than Aristotle's, though the comparison depends on the criteria chosen.

nuance.analogy: Arguably is a hedge flag: it says here is a case worth making, not a proven fact.
nuance.etymology: From arguable plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable as in 'ar-GYOO-uh-blee'.
Using it to mean certainly, when it signals that others could disagree.

senses.definition: A long-term lack of rainfall or moisture.

core.definition: A long-term lack of rainfall or moisture, so that a region's climate is very dry and few plants grow.

pronunciation.tip: Stress moves to the second syllable, RID, compared with the first-syllable stress of arid. The first syllable reduces to a quick uh, so avoid saying AIR-id-ity.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a climate or environmental condition without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use aridity in geography, ecology, agriculture, and climate discussions, and in everyday talk about living in dry regions. It is more formal than dryness. People often say 'the aridity here' when complaining about dry air in a desert city, which is a natural and common way to speak.

distinctions.note: Drought is a temporary shortage of water caused by a dry spell, while aridity is a permanent feature of a climate.
Dryness is a general quality of lacking moisture, while aridity refers to a long-term and regional climate condition.

examples.everyday: I can't get used to the aridity out here; my skin is always flaky.
examples.professional: Aridity is cutting into our crop yields in the Southwest, so we need better irrigation data before the next planting season.
examples.analytical: Aridity is best measured by the ratio of precipitation to potential evapotranspiration rather than by rainfall alone.

nuance.etymology: From Latin ariditas, dryness, from aridus.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as in AIR-id-ity, which sounds unnatural to American ears.
Using aridity for a temporary dry spell, when drought is the correct word.

senses.definition: Synonym of trooper (“a soldier of private rank in cavalry or armor”).

core.definition: A private-rank soldier serving in an armored or tank unit, sometimes called a trooper.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on AHR in armored and on SOHL in soldier. Soldier has only two syllables, so don't say sol-DEER; the final syllable is a soft, reduced jer.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive; in military contexts it suggests skill, discipline, and teamwork inside a protected vehicle.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use armored soldier as a fixed title. They more often say tanker, armor crewman, or simply soldier in an armored unit. Trooper is the traditional American term for an enlisted private in cavalry or armor, and it is the sense the dictionary gives for this phrase.

distinctions.note: Trooper is the traditional American term for an enlisted private in cavalry or armor, while armored soldier is a plain description of the role.
Tanker is a common informal term for a soldier who crews a tank, and it is more specific than armored soldier.

examples.everyday: My uncle was an armored soldier in Germany during the Cold War, and he still talks about his tank.
examples.professional: The recruiting office says the armored role needs strong mechanical skills and good teamwork.
examples.analytical: Historians describe the armored soldier of the twentieth century as a figure shaped by new machines and new forms of danger.

nuance.analogy: Like a pilot in a cockpit, the armored soldier lives and fights inside a protected machine.
nuance.etymology: Armored comes from armor (Old French armure), and soldier comes from Old French soldier, from Latin solidus (a coin used as pay).
common_mistakes: Treating armored soldier as an official rank; the actual rank is private or specialist, and armor is the branch or unit.
Pronouncing soldier with three syllables, as sol-DEER.

senses.definition: All the time, or seemingly all the time; constantly.
senses.example: They worked around the clock to finish the project on time.

core.definition: All day and all night without stopping; continuously, or seeming to never stop.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the word clock most strongly, and let around and the lose their stress. In fast speech, the and around blend into a smooth 'uh-ROWND-thuh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, but it can be positive, suggesting dedication or service, or negative, suggesting exhaustion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase for stores that stay open all night, hospitals, news coverage and people who work hard. Before a noun, it is often hyphenated as around-the-clock, as in around-the-clock care. A natural reply is 'That sounds exhausting!' or 'Wow, they never sleep.'

distinctions.note: All day covers daylight hours, while around the clock includes the night as well.
24/7 is common in business and tech writing, while around the clock sounds more spoken or journalistic.
Nonstop emphasizes that there is no pause, while around the clock emphasizes covering both day and night.

examples.everyday: The gas station on Main Street is open around the clock, so we can grab milk any time.
examples.professional: Our support team covers customer issues around the clock by rotating shifts across three time zones.
examples.analytical: The surveillance system records around the clock, which raises questions about privacy and the limits of consent.

nuance.analogy: Like a lighthouse that keeps shining through both day and night.
nuance.etymology: From around (encircling) plus clock, referring to one full cycle of the clock's hours.
common_mistakes: Using around the clock only for nighttime; it means day and night together.
Writing around the clocks with a plural; the phrase is singular.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to artisans or the work of artisans.
senses.example: The coffee shop serves artisanal pastries baked each morning by a small local team.

senses.definition: Involving skilled work, with comparatively little reliance on machinery.
senses.example: She prefers artisanal soap made in small batches without industrial machinery.

senses.definition: Made by an artisan (skilled worker).

core.definition: Made by skilled craftspeople, usually by hand and in small batches, rather than mass-produced by machines.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on ZAN, with a short a like in 'cat'. Do not stress the first syllable as in the noun 'artisan', and do not use a short i in the middle.

nuance.connotation: Positive, suggesting quality and craft; marketing overuse can make it sound inflated or pretentious.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use this word for food, drinks, coffee, soap and crafts, such as 'artisanal bread' at a farmers market. It is a marketing word, so it is common on menus and labels. In everyday speech, 'handmade' or 'homemade' can be simpler and more natural.

distinctions.note: Handmade means made by hand at any scale; artisanal implies a skilled craft tradition and often a small producer.
Craft is broader and can mean a skill, a hobby or an industry; artisanal describes the method and quality of a product.
Gourmet describes high quality of food or taste; artisanal describes how something was made.

examples.everyday: I'll grab a loaf of that artisanal sourdough from the farmers market on the way home.
examples.professional: Our marketing team wants to position the brand as artisanal, so we need to explain how each product is made.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that the artisanal label often hides industrial production on a much larger scale.

nuance.analogy: Like a hand-thrown clay pot compared with one stamped out on an assembly line.
nuance.etymology: From artisan, borrowed from French and Italian (artigiano), with the adjective suffix -al.
common_mistakes: Using 'artisanal' as a noun, as in 'an artisanal' for a craftsperson; the correct noun is 'artisan'.
Pronouncing it with a short i in the middle (ar-ti-ZAN-al) instead of ar-tuh-ZAN-uhl.

senses.definition: In an artless manner.

core.definition: In a simple, sincere way, without tricks, pretense, or any attempt to impress.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, ART. The middle syllable is a syllabic l, so say three clear syllables with no extra vowel after the t: 'ART-lis-lee,' not 'ar-tuh-less-lee.'

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral, suggesting openness and sincerity; it can sound slightly negative if it implies naivety or clumsiness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use artlessly in speech. It appears mainly in writing, reviews, and literary description, as in 'she smiled artlessly.' In conversation, say 'innocently' or 'without trying to impress anyone' instead. It describes the manner of an action, not the person.

distinctions.note: Innocently suggests no bad intent, often about actions with unintended effects; artlessly stresses natural openness without pretense.
Naively implies a lack of judgment or experience; artlessly is neutral or warm.
Sincerely describes meaning what you say; artlessly describes the unpretentious manner of an action.

examples.everyday: He told me artlessly that he had forgotten my birthday again, which somehow made it funnier.
examples.professional: When the intern admitted he didn't know the answer, he spoke artlessly, and the team respected him for it.
examples.analytical: The narrator describes the village artlessly, yet the careful detail reveals a sharply observed social hierarchy.

nuance.analogy: Artlessly is like a child drawing a house with crooked lines: the honesty shows, and nothing is staged.
nuance.etymology: From artless plus -ly; artless from art 'craft, cunning' plus -less 'without'.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra vowel, as in 'ar-tuh-less-lee.'
Using it in casual speech, where 'innocently' or 'openly' sounds more natural.

senses.definition: Moving upward; ascending, rising.
senses.example: The hot air balloon was ascendant, drifting steadily upward over the green valley.

senses.definition: Controlling, dominant, surpassing.
senses.example: By the late 1990s, the company had become the ascendant player in regional logistics.

senses.definition: In an eastern direction rising just above the horizon.
senses.example: Astronomers noted that Jupiter was ascendant just before dawn, low above the eastern horizon.

senses.definition: Synonym of ascending (“of or pertaining to one's ancestors”).
senses.example: The genealogy chart showed the ascendant line from her parents back through four generations.

senses.definition: Rising towards the zenith.
senses.example: The sun was ascendant toward its zenith as the hikers reached the summit at noon.

senses.definition: Of a part of an organism: synonym of ascending (“leading or sloping upwards”).
senses.example: The ascendant branch of the plant's stem curved gently toward the window light.

senses.definition: The degree of the zodiac or point of the ecliptic which rises in an eastern direction above the horizon at a particular moment (especially the moment of a person's birth), which is supposed to have a commanding influence on a person's fortune and life; a horoscope.
senses.example: My astrologer insisted that my ascendant in Scorpio explained my stubbornness.

senses.definition: Chiefly in in the ascendant: an act of ascending or rising.
senses.example: After the merger, the younger team was firmly in the ascendant.

senses.definition: Synonym of ascendancy (“commanding influence; dominant control; superiority, supremacy”).
senses.example: One man has the ascendant over another.

senses.definition: An ancestor.
senses.example: Our family's ascendants came from Ireland in the 1850s, according to old letters.

senses.definition: A person who ascends or goes up; specifically (usually followed by to), a person who ascends to a throne or assumes some other position of power.
senses.example: Given his father’s ghastly demise, one would not expect such glee from the ascendant to his throne.

senses.definition: Something which is higher than the things around it; a peak, a summit; specifically, synonym of ascender (“the portion of a lowercase letter that extends above the midline”).
senses.example: In the printed font, the ascendant of the letter h rises above the x-height.

senses.definition: Something which leads or slopes upwards, such as a flight of stairs or an upward incline.
senses.example: The hikers paused at the ascendant, catching their breath before the final climb.

senses.definition: (rare) A person who supports a policy of ecclesiastical or national supremacy.
senses.example: The pamphlet branded him an ascendant, a zealous champion of royal supremacy over the church.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Rising in power, influence, or popularity; becoming more dominant and gaining ground over others.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, SEN. The final '-ant' is a reduced 'unt', not the insect word 'ant', which many learners wrongly pronounce.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes someone or something gaining strength, usually with admiration or a sense of momentum.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use 'ascendant' in the set phrase 'in the ascendant,' in writing, journalism, and formal commentary. In casual speech they would say 'on the rise' or 'taking off' instead. Astrology uses the same word for a rising sign, which is a specialized sense.

distinctions.note: Ascendant is the adjective describing a rising force, while ascendancy is the noun for the state of dominance itself.
'On the rise' is casual and everyday, while 'ascendant' is formal and suggests growing dominance rather than just growth.
Dominant describes a current position of control, while ascendant describes the process of gaining that control.

examples.everyday: Her new podcast is in the ascendant, and half the people at my gym now listen to it.
examples.professional: Our open-source tools are now ascendant in the team, so the proprietary vendor is losing ground.
examples.analytical: Reformist ideas became ascendant in the nineteenth-century parliament once the franchise widened.

nuance.analogy: Like a kite rising on a strong wind, climbing higher and higher than the others.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ascendere 'to climb up', through Old French and Middle English.
common_mistakes: Using 'ascendant' as a verb, as in 'the team ascendant'; it is an adjective or noun.
Pronouncing it with a stressed 'ant' like the insect, instead of a reduced final syllable.

ascendant.etymology: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English *ascendent* (“ascending, rising; increasing in quantity; rising above the horizon”), borrowed from Old French *ascendant*, from Latin *ascendentem*, the accusative singular of *ascendēns* (“ascending,…

senses.definition: Away from the proper path; in a wrong or unknown direction.
senses.example: The shipment went astray somewhere between Chicago and Denver last week.

senses.definition: Away from what is right and good; into error or evil.
senses.example: Years of pressure from his friends led him astray, and he never quite recovered.

core.definition: Off the right path or course; into error, trouble, or wrongdoing.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, STRAY. Americans pronounce the r clearly and do not add a t sound between s and r; the word sounds like 'uh-STRAY,' with no 'uh-STRAY-t'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or cautionary. It suggests something has gone wrong, been lost, or led someone into error.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use astray in the phrases 'go astray' and 'lead astray.' 'Go astray' is used for plans, mail, or data that do not arrive or work as expected. 'Lead astray' is used for people who are misled or tempted into bad behavior, and it is somewhat literary. In everyday talk, 'get lost' or 'go wrong' is more common.

distinctions.note: Lost means you do not know where you are or cannot find something; astray suggests you have left the right path or intended course.
Stray is used as an adjective or verb, as in 'a stray dog'; astray is used only as an adverb, mostly after 'go' or 'lead'.
Adrift means floating or drifting without direction; astray suggests going wrong from a proper route or standard.

examples.everyday: My package went astray in the mail, so I'm waiting on a replacement from the seller.
examples.professional: A sensor fault sent some readings astray, so we removed those records before running the analysis.
examples.analytical: Augustine argued that human desire, when misdirected, leads the will astray from its proper end in God.

nuance.analogy: Like a river that leaves its channel and floods the fields instead of reaching the sea.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English a- (on, in) plus stray, from Old French estraier 'to wander', from Late Latin extravagari 'to wander outside'.
common_mistakes: Writing 'a stray' or 'in astray' when you mean 'astray'; the adverb has no article and is not preceded by 'in.'
Using 'astray' for a physical place you are simply lost in; 'lost' is the normal word for that.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew shagah means to err or go astray, and the Greek planaō means to wander or lead astray. Isaiah 53:6 says that all people have turned away like sheep, each going his own way. Matthew 18:12 uses the parable of the lost sheep to show that God seeks the one that has gone astray. Psalm 119:176 uses the image of a lost sheep to express the psalmist's plea to be found again.

astray.etymology: From Middle English *astraien* or by apheresis *straien*, from Old French *estraier* (“to stray”), from late Medieval Latin *extravagari* (“to wander beyond”), from Latin *extra* (“beyond”) + *vagārī* (“to wander, stray”).

senses.definition: To make reparation, compensation, amends or satisfaction for an offense, crime, mistake or deficiency.
senses.example: He tried to atone for his mistakes by working harder.

senses.definition: To absolve (someone else) of wrongdoing, especially by standing as an equivalent.
senses.example: Scripture teaches that Christ died to atone for the sins of humankind.

core.definition: To make up for a wrong you did, by apologizing, making amends, or accepting a cost or punishment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the single syllable TOHN, which rhymes with 'phone' and 'own'. The first syllable is a weak schwa, so do not say it as a full 'a' sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive in the sense that it shows responsibility, but serious. It implies that the wrong was significant and that the person accepts a real cost to repair it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in casual speech, where they say 'make up for it' or 'make it right'. You will hear it in serious discussions, in religious contexts, in news reports about public apologies, or in formal writing. The usual preposition is 'atone for', as in 'atone for a mistake'.

distinctions.note: Apologize means to say you are sorry, while atone means to take action to repair the harm, which can include a cost or sacrifice.
Repent emphasizes an inner change of heart and turning away from wrongdoing, often in a religious setting, while atone emphasizes making amends.
Compensate means to give money or something of value to make up for a loss, while atone also carries moral and personal meaning.

collocations: spend a lifetime trying to atone

examples.everyday: He spent the whole weekend cooking and cleaning to atone for forgetting my birthday.
examples.professional: The company agreed to atone for the outage by issuing credits to every affected customer and publishing a full postmortem.
examples.analytical: Many philosophers ask whether suffering can ever truly atone for a wrong done to another person.

nuance.analogy: Like paying back a debt you owe for damage you caused, plus whatever interest the other person needs to feel made whole.
nuance.etymology: From the phrase 'at one', meaning in agreement or reconciled, formed in the sixteenth century.
common_mistakes: Using 'atone of' instead of 'atone for'.
Using atone as a casual synonym for 'say sorry', when it requires making amends.

senses.definition: Connected; joined.
senses.example: The car has something of a history attached to it.

senses.definition: Fond of (used with to).
senses.example: I'm very attached to my pets.

senses.definition: Included as an attachment with a communication (especially an email or other electronic communication).
senses.example: Please see the attached file in my previous email.

senses.definition: In a romantic or sexual relationship.
senses.example: As far as I know, he isn't attached, so I'm going to invite him out on a date.

senses.definition: Of a residential building, sharing walls with similar buildings on two, usually opposite, sides.
senses.example: They bought an attached row house with a narrow back garden and a shared wall.

senses.definition: Broadly joined to a stem or stipe, but not decurrent.
senses.example: In this group of mushrooms, the attachment of the gills to the stipe ranges from attached to almost decurrent.

core.definition: Fastened or joined to something; or emotionally close to someone or something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, TACHT. The -ed is pronounced as a t sound because it follows ch, so the word has only two syllables. Do not add an extra syllable at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical and email use. In personal use it is warm, suggesting a close bond with a person, place or object.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use attached in two common ways: physically fastened, as in the attached file in an email, and emotionally connected, as in I'm attached to this old sweater. In emails, Americans write Please find the file attached or I've attached the report. To say you like someone a lot in a relationship, Americans more often say they are close or serious.

distinctions.note: Fond expresses a warm liking; attached suggests a stronger, longer-lasting bond or dependence.
Connected is broader and can describe ideas or systems; attached usually means fastened or closely bound.

examples.everyday: I'm really attached to this old couch, even though it's falling apart.
examples.professional: I've attached the revised forecast to this email, so please check the Q3 numbers before Friday.
examples.analytical: Augustine argued that the human will is attached to its desires in ways that reason cannot easily undo.

nuance.analogy: Being attached is like a magnet and a fridge: the connection is strong enough that it doesn't come off with a light push.
nuance.etymology: From attach, from Old French atachier, meaning to fasten.
common_mistakes: Using attached with the wrong preposition: say attached to, not attached with or attached at.
Pronouncing the final -ed as a separate syllable, saying uh-TACH-ed.

senses.definition: A poem or song evoking or greeting the dawn or early morning.
A morning love song, or a song of lovers parting in the morning.
A concert held at dawn or in the morning, especially outdoors.
senses.example: The church choir performed an aubade on the lakeshore as the sun rose over the water.

core.definition: A poem or song that greets the dawn, or a song of lovers parting in the morning.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, and the final d is a clear consonant, not a vowel like 'ahd'. The vowel is the open 'ah' of American 'cot'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. The word is lyrical and romantic, and it appears mostly in poetry and literary criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Most Americans have never used this word in conversation, so you will meet it in poetry classes, literary essays, or concert listings. Do not use it in everyday talk, where 'morning song' or 'dawn poem' is clearer. You might hear it in a classical-music context, for a concert held at sunrise.

distinctions.note: A serenade is a song sung to a beloved, traditionally in the evening, while an aubade is set at dawn.
A nocturne evokes night, while an aubade evokes the morning.

examples.everyday: Nobody I know says aubade, but my roommate's poetry class had us read one about sunrise.
examples.professional: The program notes describe the sunrise concert as an aubade, so plan to arrive by six.
examples.analytical: Donne's 'The Sun Rising' parodies the aubade by scolding the sun for interrupting two lovers in bed.

nuance.analogy: Think of it as the morning version of a serenade.
nuance.etymology: From Old Provençal 'alba', dawn, through French 'aubade'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as in 'AW-bayd'.
Pronouncing the final d as a vowel, or the ending like 'parade'.
Using it in everyday speech where 'morning song' would be more natural.

senses.definition: Showing willingness to take bold risks; recklessly daring.
Impudent, insolent.
senses.example: Her audacious reply to the manager got her sent home early that afternoon.

core.definition: Willing to take bold risks; daring, sometimes to the point of recklessness, or sometimes rudely bold.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on DAY, the second syllable. The ending '-ious' is pronounced 'shus', not 'see-us'. Don't confuse it with 'audacity', which is stressed on the middle syllable.

nuance.connotation: Mixed. It is positive for bold ideas and goals, and negative when it means impudent or reckless behavior.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'audacious' for bold business plans, ambitious goals, or a daring move, often with admiration. It can also describe rude behavior, as in 'an audacious kid who talks back to the teacher.' In casual speech, 'bold' or 'ballsy' is more common, so 'audacious' sounds a bit elevated.

distinctions.note: Bold is everyday and mostly positive, while audacious adds surprise and a sense that the act is almost too daring.
Reckless is always negative and means careless of danger, while audacious can praise a risk that was well chosen.

examples.everyday: Asking for a free upgrade at the hotel was audacious, but it actually worked.
examples.professional: Leadership approved an audacious goal of cutting our model's latency by 80 percent this quarter.
examples.analytical: Descartes makes the audacious claim that the mind can doubt everything except its own act of doubting.

nuance.analogy: Like a tightrope walker who goes without a net: impressive, but a fall could be serious.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'audax', bold, from 'audere', to dare.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable as in 'aw-DAH-shus'.
Confusing it with 'audible', which means able to be heard.
Using it for simple courage in everyday talk, where 'brave' or 'bold' is more natural.

audacious.etymology: From Latin *audacia* (“boldness”) + *-ious*, from *audax* (“bold”), from *audeō* (“to be bold, to dare”).

senses.definition: A diviner who foretells events by the behavior of birds or other animals, or by signs derived from celestial phenomena, or unusual occurrences.
senses.example: The ancient augur studied the flight of birds before advising the general to march.

senses.definition: An official who interpreted omens before the start of public events.
senses.example: Before the senate voted, the augur read the omens from the sky.

senses.definition: To foretell events; to exhibit signs of future events; to indicate a favorable or an unfavorable outcome.
senses.example: Every circumstance augured success.

core.definition: To be a sign of how something will turn out; to predict a result, good or bad.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a reduced American 'er' with no separate vowel. Non-native speakers often add a clear 'oo' or a second syllable, so keep it to one stressed syllable plus a quick 'er'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. Often used with 'well' or 'ill' ('augurs well'), so the tone depends on the second word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'augur' mostly in formal writing or in set phrases like 'augur well for' or 'augur badly for'. In everyday speech, 'bode well' or 'look good' is more common. Replying 'Yeah, that sounds promising' is a natural response to someone who says it augurs well.

distinctions.note: 'Predict' is neutral and direct, while 'augur' implies a sign or an early indication that points toward an outcome.
'Bode' is nearly always used with 'well' or 'ill', while 'augur' can also stand alone as a transitive verb meaning to foretell.

examples.everyday: The way the kids cleaned their rooms without being asked really augurs well for the weekend.
examples.professional: The strong pilot results augur well for our launch next quarter, so let's plan the rollout.
examples.analytical: Early empirical evidence may augur well for the theory, but it cannot settle the question of causation.

nuance.analogy: Like dark clouds on the horizon, an augur is a sign that points toward what is coming.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'augurare', to practice augury, from 'augur', a diviner who interpreted birds.
common_mistakes: Using 'augur' as a noun for a simple prediction, when it refers to a diviner or to an omen.
Forgetting that 'augur' usually needs 'well' or 'ill' or 'for' to be natural in everyday speech.

augur.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *augur*, of uncertain origin; akin to *augurō* (“interpret omens”).

senses.definition: The originator or creator of a work, especially of a literary composition; or, one of the creators of a collaborative work.
senses.example: The copyright of any original writing belongs initially and properly to its author.

senses.definition: Someone who writes books for a living.
The creator or cause of anything.
The initial owner of the copyright to a work, especially a work made for hire or a work of corporate authorship.
senses.example: The author named on the copyright registration for the Android robot is Google Inc.

senses.definition: To create a work as its author.

core.definition: The person who wrote a book, article, report or other written work, or one of the people who wrote it together.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle sound is a voiceless th, as in 'thing', not a t; the last syllable is weak, like 'er'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It names the creator of a work and carries respect for the writing, though it is neutral in ordinary use.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in all settings: 'Who's the author of this report?' or 'I love that author.' Calling a woman an authoress sounds dated and is avoided. The verb 'to author' is also common in corporate and technical writing, as in 'She authored the proposal.'

distinctions.note: Writer is broader and can describe a profession or skill; author suggests the creator of a specific published work.
Novelist refers only to someone who writes novels; author covers books, articles and academic writing of any kind.

examples.everyday: Have you read anything by that author? My sister says her mystery novels are hard to put down.
examples.professional: Please list the author and co-author on the slide deck before we send it to the client on Friday.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the text's ambiguity is deliberate, inviting readers to supply the missing link themselves.

nuance.analogy: Like an architect whose design comes first, before any bricks are laid.
nuance.etymology: From Old French autor, from Latin auctor 'originator, promoter', from augere 'to increase'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle sound as a t, as in AH-ter; the sound is a voiceless th.
Writing authoress for a female writer; most Americans just say author.

author.etymology: From Middle English *auctour*, from Anglo-Norman *autour*, from Old French *autor*, from Latin *auctor*, from *augeō* (“to increase, originate”).

senses.definition: The process of making an action of a higher animal reflexive.
senses.example: Years of piano practice led to automatization, so she no longer thought about finger placement.

senses.definition: Automation.

core.definition: The process of making a task or process run automatically, with little human effort or conscious control; automation.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on ZAY, the -ation syllable. The word is four syllables before the stress, so keep the earlier syllables light and unstressed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical writing. In public debate it can carry worry about job loss, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost always say 'automation' in everyday and business speech. 'Automatization' appears mainly in psychology, where it means a skill becoming automatic through practice, and in some academic or British writing. In a US workplace, 'automation' is the word people will recognize immediately.

distinctions.note: Automation is the everyday American term for the same idea; automatization is more formal and is used more in psychology and scholarly prose.
Mechanization means replacing human labor with machines; automatization can also mean making a human skill habitual through practice.

examples.everyday: My uncle works at a factory and says the automatization of the line has changed everything about his job.
examples.professional: The team's proposal focuses on the automatization of our reporting workflow, so the analysts can spend time on interpretation.
examples.analytical: Her essay argues that the automatization of skilled labor changes not only productivity but also the moral texture of work.

nuance.analogy: Like a path worn across a field: the more people walk it, the more the route runs on its own.
nuance.etymology: From automatize, from automatic, from Greek automatos 'self-acting'.
common_mistakes: Using 'automatization' in casual American speech where 'automation' is expected.
Pronouncing the stress on the early syllables instead of on ZAY.

senses.definition: An autoregressive process that is used to model many types of natural behavior.
senses.example: We fit an autoregression of order three to capture the weekly pattern in sales.

core.definition: A statistical model that predicts a variable's future value as a weighted sum of its own past values plus random error.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, AW, with a weaker secondary stress on greh. The ending is -shun, not -see-un, and the r in the middle is pronounced because American English is rhotic.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term mainly in statistics, econometrics, data science, and economics courses. Outside those fields it is unfamiliar, so in a mixed audience say 'a model that predicts from its own past values' first. Colleagues usually shorten it to 'AR model' or simply 'AR' when speaking.

distinctions.note: Ordinary regression predicts an outcome from separate predictor variables, while autoregression predicts a series from its own earlier values.
An MA model uses past forecast errors, whereas an autoregression uses past values of the series itself.
ARIMA combines autoregression, differencing to remove trends, and a moving average component in one model.

examples.everyday: My coworker said the sales forecast is basically an autoregression, so it mostly just looks at last month's numbers.
examples.professional: I'll fit an autoregression on the weekly demand data and check the residuals before we present the forecast.
examples.analytical: A first-order autoregression assumes that each observation depends linearly on the immediately preceding value plus white noise.

nuance.analogy: Like predicting your mood today mostly from how you felt yesterday, plus some random day-to-day noise.
nuance.etymology: From auto- (self, from Greek autos) and regression (from Latin regressio, 'a going back').
common_mistakes: Confusing autoregression with ordinary regression, which uses separate predictor variables rather than the series' own past values.
Stressing the second syllable, as in aw-TOH-ruh-gression, instead of AW-toh-ruh-greh-shun.

senses.definition: To operate an aircraft.

core.definition: To fly an aircraft; to operate or pilot an airplane or other flying machine.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, AY. The final syllable rhymes with late, with a light secondary stress, so the word has three clear beats.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a formal or technical term, sometimes used with humor.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use aviate in conversation. They would say fly a plane or pilot an aircraft. You will see aviate in aviation writing, military contexts, or in a playful tone. The noun aviator and aviation are much more common.

distinctions.note: Fly is the everyday word for moving through the air in an aircraft. Aviate is more formal and focuses on the skill of piloting.
Pilot is the common verb for operating an aircraft in both everyday and professional speech. Aviate is more formal and rare.

examples.everyday: My neighbor learned to aviate small planes years ago, and he still flies over the lake on weekends.
examples.professional: The training syllabus requires cadets to aviate solo before they navigate cross-country flights.
examples.analytical: To aviate is to master a three-dimensional environment that gives little room for error, and that discipline shapes a pilot's judgment.

nuance.analogy: Like a sailor who learns to steer a boat through wind and current: aviating is steering through the air.
nuance.etymology: Back-formed from aviation, from French aviation, from Latin avis 'bird'.
common_mistakes: Using aviate in everyday speech where fly or pilot is the natural choice.
Stressing the second syllable or pronouncing the final syllable with a short vowel.

senses.definition: A hobby or recreational or leisure pursuit.
senses.example: Woodworking is his avocation, and he spends weekends building furniture for friends.

senses.definition: That which calls one away from one's regular employment or vocation.
senses.example: Politics became an avocation that gradually pulled him away from his regular law practice.

senses.definition: Pursuits; duties; affairs which occupy one's time; usual employment; vocation.
senses.example: Between her avocations at the church and the school, she rarely had a free evening.

senses.definition: The calling of a case from an inferior to a superior court.
senses.example: The appellate judge granted the avocation of the case from the county court to the state supreme court.

core.definition: An activity you do for enjoyment in your spare time, separate from your paid job.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on 'kay,' with a light secondary stress on the first syllable. Keep the middle vowel as a clear 'oh' and avoid shortening it to a schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests a personal interest that gives meaning outside work.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use avocation in formal writing, bios, or polite conversation, but in everyday speech they usually say hobby or 'what I do for fun.' It can sound a bit stiff in casual talk, though it is natural in a professional bio or a formal interview. Avocation often implies a serious, long-term interest.

distinctions.note: A hobby is the everyday word for a leisure activity, while avocation is more formal and can suggest a deeper, serious pursuit.
A vocation is your paid work or calling, while an avocation is an unpaid interest you pursue outside it.

examples.everyday: What do you do for fun? Painting is my hobby, and I guess it's my real avocation too.
examples.professional: In the bio, the speaker described astronomy as her avocation alongside her work in data engineering.
examples.analytical: Aristotle's idea of leisure suggests that the highest human activity is not a vocation but an avocation pursued for its own sake.

nuance.analogy: Your vocation pays the bills, and your avocation fills your weekends.
nuance.etymology: From Latin avocare, 'to call away,' from a- ('away') and vocare ('to call').
common_mistakes: Confusing avocation with vocation, so that a paid job is described as a hobby.
Confusing avocation with advocacy, which means active support for a cause.

avocation.etymology: From Latin *āvocātiō* (“a distraction”), from *āvocō* (“to call off, distract”).

senses.definition: The quality or degree of being bad.

core.definition: The quality or degree of being bad, whether in poor quality, unpleasant conditions, or moral wrongness.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BAD. The final -ness is a reduced schwa and s, not a long vowel, and the n is pronounced clearly before the schwa.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it names a bad quality or condition, usually in an abstract way.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech people usually say how bad something is or the bad part, rather than using badness. The noun appears more often in writing about quality, morality or abstract conditions. A casual reply to the badness of the weather is Tell me about it.

distinctions.note: Evil is a stronger moral term for deliberate wrongdoing, while badness can describe anything from a movie to a moral failing.
Wickedness is formal and stresses deliberate malice, while badness is broader and more neutral.
Awfulness is informal and describes how unpleasant something is, often for emphasis.

collocations: a mix of goodness and badness

examples.everyday: The badness of the traffic made us miss the first half of the game.
examples.professional: The root cause analysis showed that the badness of the release came from a caching error.
examples.analytical: Augustine treats the badness of evil not as a substance but as a privation of good.

nuance.analogy: Like a dimmer switch: badness is less light, not a separate kind of darkness.
nuance.etymology: From bad plus the suffix -ness, from Old English -nes, forming abstract nouns.
common_mistakes: Using badness to describe a person directly, as in he is a badness: say he is bad or his behavior is bad.
Confusing badness with badly, which is an adverb: write the badness of the plan, not the badly of the plan.

core.definition: A eunuch and chief officer of the Assyrian general Holofernes in the book of Judith, who is in charge of his master's affairs and his tent.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, BAY. The final syllable is a reduced vowel, so do not pronounce it as a full 'ah' sound or as 'ass'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a name from a biblical narrative, not an emotionally loaded word.
nuance.usage_note: Bagoas appears mainly in Bible study, church teaching and academic discussions of Judith. Americans would say the name in the same way they say other names from Scripture, and in conversation you would usually add context such as 'the eunuch in Judith' so people know which Bagoas you mean.

distinctions.note: Bigvai is a different biblical name, a post-exilic family head in Ezra and Nehemiah, so do not confuse the two names in a sermon or paper.

examples.everyday: In the Bible study last night we talked about Bagoas, the eunuch who serves Holofernes in the book of Judith.
examples.professional: When I preach from Judith, I introduce Bagoas early so the congregation understands his role as the official who manages Holofernes' household.
examples.analytical: In Judith 12:11, Bagoas is identified as the eunuch who has charge of all Holofernes' affairs, a detail that establishes his close access to the general.

nuance.analogy: Bagoas is like a chief of staff who controls his commander's schedule and access, so his position matters more than his title suggests.
nuance.etymology: Bagoas is a Greek form of an old Persian name, possibly related to Bagauš; the exact meaning is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as a full 'ahs' sound instead of a reduced 'us'.
Confusing Bagoas with Bigvai, a different name in Ezra and Nehemiah.
Assuming Bagoas appears in all Bibles; Judith is in the Apocrypha or deuterocanonical books, which Protestant Bibles omit.
nuance.biblical_note: Bagoas is a eunuch in the book of Judith, a narrative set in the time of Nebuchadnezzar, who serves as chief officer over the Assyrian general Holofernes. He takes charge of Holofernes' affairs and is present when Judith comes to the camp, which makes him a key figure in the story. Judith 12:11 describes him as the eunuch in charge of all his master's affairs. Historically, a Persian eunuch named Bagoas also appears in Greek sources as a powerful court official. Judith is included in the Catholic and Orthodox canons but is in the Apocrypha for Protestants.

senses.definition: Any substance, especially food, used in catching fish, or other animals, by alluring them to a hook, snare, trap, or net.
senses.example: attach bait to a hook

senses.definition: Food containing poison or a harmful additive to kill animals that are pests.
senses.example: The farm store sells bait containing rat poison, so keep it away from the dog.

senses.definition: Anything which allures; something or someone used to lure or entice someone or something into doing something.
senses.example: clickbait

senses.definition: A post intended to elicit a, usually strong or negative, reaction from others.
senses.example: Please stop posting bait, or I will have to mute you.

senses.definition: Something that lures or entices a specified group.
senses.example: queerbait

senses.definition: Someone that attracts or entices a specified sex act being done to them.
senses.example: somno bait

senses.definition: A portion of food or drink, as a refreshment taken on a journey; also, a stop for rest and refreshment.
senses.example: We stopped at a roadside diner for a quick bait of coffee and pie before driving on.

senses.definition: A small meal taken mid-morning while farming.
senses.example: Before the sun got hot, the farmhands gathered under the oak for their mid-morning bait.

senses.definition: A light or hasty luncheon.
senses.example: Since the meeting ran long, we grabbed a light bait at the deli before the afternoon session.

senses.definition: To attract with bait; to entice.
senses.example: Advertisers often bait shoppers with discounts that disappear once they reach the register.

senses.definition: To affix bait to a trap or a fishing hook or fishing line.
senses.example: Before casting, my grandfather would carefully bait the hook with a live worm.

senses.definition: To lay baits in an environment to control pest species.
senses.example: The county crews bait the fields each spring to control the rodent population.

senses.definition: To target a pest species by laying baits.
senses.example: Wildlife biologists bait raccoons near the orchard to reduce the spread of rabies.

senses.definition: To set dogs on (an animal etc.) to bite or worry; to attack with dogs, especially for sport.
senses.example: to bait a bear with dogs

senses.definition: To intentionally annoy, torment, or threaten by constant rebukes or threats; to harass.
senses.example: For years, the bully would bait the new kid with cruel nicknames during lunch.

senses.definition: Of a horse or other animal: to take food, especially during a journey.
senses.example: The mare began to bait along the trail, nibbling grass whenever the rider slowed.

senses.definition: (of a person) To stop to take a portion of food and drink for refreshment during a journey.
senses.example: We decided to bait at the rest stop near Flagstaff before the long climb.

senses.definition: Obvious; blatant.
Well-known; famous; renowned.

core.definition: Food or another substance used to attract fish or animals so they can be caught in a hook, trap, or net.

pronunciation.tip: This is a single syllable that rhymes with 'gate' and 'late'. Learners sometimes say it like 'bite,' so keep the vowel as a clear long 'ay' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in fishing and hunting, but negative when it is used to describe deliberately luring someone into a trap or argument.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bait most often in fishing and hunting, such as 'Did you buy worms for bait?' The word is also common in everyday speech for trickery, as in 'Don't take the bait,' meaning don't react to someone trying to provoke you. In a store or restaurant context, the word is rarely used, so do not use it to describe food in general.
