nuance.etymology: From Latin discernere, from dis- (apart) plus cernere 'to separate, sift'.
common_mistakes: Using 'discern' as a noun; the noun is 'discernment'.
Using 'discern from' instead of 'discern between' or 'discern the difference'.
Pronouncing it as dis-ERN, with the stress on the first syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek words behind 'discern' include diakrinō, meaning to distinguish or separate, and dokimazō, meaning to test or approve. 1 Corinthians 12:10 lists the discerning of spirits as a gift. Hebrews 5:14 speaks of mature believers whose senses are trained to distinguish good from evil. Romans 12:2 encourages believers to test and discern what the will of God is.

discern.etymology: From Middle English *discernen*, from Old French *discerner*, from Latin *discernere* (“to separate, divide, distinguish, discern”), from *dis-* (“apart”) + *cernere* (“to distinguish”); see certain.

senses.definition: Of, pertaining to, or arising from disposition (in any sense)
senses.example: dispositional optimism

core.definition: Relating to a person's stable character traits or inclinations, or to an arrangement of things.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'ZISH'. The ending '-al' is reduced to a light 'ul' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term in philosophy and psychology.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'dispositional' mainly in academic writing in philosophy and psychology, for example 'dispositional traits.' In everyday speech, people would say 'personality traits' or 'tendencies' instead.

distinctions.note: 'Dispositional' describes stable internal traits; 'situational' describes behavior caused by the circumstances.
'Personal' is general and everyday; 'dispositional' is precise and technical.

examples.everyday: Some people are just dispositional optimists, so they always see the bright side.
examples.professional: The HR report separated dispositional factors from the team's current workload.
examples.analytical: A dispositional account of belief explains knowledge in terms of a person's stable tendencies.

nuance.analogy: A dispositional trait is like a spring in a clock: it is built in and shows itself when the right pressure is applied.
nuance.etymology: From 'disposition' plus the suffix '-al,' from Latin 'dispositio.'
common_mistakes: Using it as a noun instead of an adjective.
Confusing it with 'situational' in psychology discussions.

senses.definition: Lack of quiet; absence of tranquility in body or mind.
senses.example: A growing disquiet settled over the family as the storm approached and the power flickered.

senses.definition: To make (someone or something) worried or anxious.
senses.example: He felt disquieted by the lack of interest the child had shown.

core.definition: A feeling of worry, unease, or restlessness that makes it hard to feel calm.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on -KWY-, and the final syllable is a reduced vowel, not a full 'it'. Non-native speakers often stress the last syllable or pronounce the 'qu' as 'k' alone.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes an uneasy feeling of anxiety or worry, often without a clear cause.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use disquiet mostly in writing or formal speech, especially news reports and literature. In everyday talk they usually say worry, unease, or anxiety. A typical everyday phrase is 'a sense of unease', which sounds more natural than the noun form.

distinctions.note: Anxiety is a common, often clinical word for persistent worry. Disquiet is more literary and usually describes a general feeling of unease that may be vague.
Unrest describes social or political disturbance or a group's agitation. Disquiet is an individual or general feeling of worry.

examples.everyday: I felt a sense of disquiet when my daughter didn't text back after her flight landed.
examples.professional: There is growing disquiet among the team about the rushed deadline.
examples.analytical: The essay traces a modern disquiet, a restless suspicion that our institutions no longer answer to shared purposes.

nuance.analogy: Disquiet is like a radio slightly out of tune, with a faint hum that never quite stops, so you cannot fully relax.
nuance.etymology: From Old French desquiete, from Latin inquietus, not quiet, with the prefix dis- meaning opposite.
common_mistakes: Using disquiet as a count noun with 'a disquiet' for many separate events; it is usually uncountable.
Stressing the last syllable: say dihs-KWY-uht, not dihs-kwy-EHT.

senses.definition: The quality of being distributive.

core.definition: The property of an operation that lets it be spread across a sum or combination, such as a times (b plus c) equaling ab plus ac.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on TIV, the third syllable, and the final -ity is pronounced 'uh-tee'. Avoid stressing the first syllable, and keep the reduced vowels in the middle syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise mathematical term.
nuance.usage_note: In American math classes this word appears when students learn about multiplication across addition. Outside mathematics and logic it is very rare. Americans usually just say 'the distributive property' in school, and 'distributivity' is the more formal term in research.

distinctions.note: The distributive property is the common school term for the rule; distributivity is the abstract concept of having that property.
Associativity concerns grouping of operations; distributivity concerns how one operation spreads over another.

examples.everyday: My son asked why 3 times 12 is the same as 3 times 10 plus 3 times 2, and I said it is distributivity.
examples.professional: We checked distributivity of the operator, since our proof depends on it holding across the matrix product.
examples.analytical: Whether the structure has distributivity determines whether it qualifies as a ring rather than a weaker algebraic object.

nuance.analogy: Like splitting a shopping bill into two parts and paying each part at the same rate: the total is the same whichever way you split it.
nuance.etymology: From distributive, from Latin distributivus, plus the abstract noun ending -ity.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'distributivity' with 'distribution', which is a different word and concept.
Using it casually when 'the distributive property' is the expected phrase in school.

senses.definition: To strip, deprive, or dispossess (someone) of something (such as a right, passion, privilege, or prejudice).
senses.example: You shall never divest me of my right to free speech.

senses.definition: To sell off or be rid of through sale, especially of a subsidiary.
senses.example: In 2011, the company divested an 81% majority stake in its foreign subsidiary.

core.definition: To remove something from someone, such as a right, power or property, or to sell off an investment or business unit.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, so keep the first syllable light and quick. Don't confuse it with "divest" sounding like "divorce" or with "invest," which is a different verb.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in finance and business; can feel negative when someone is stripped of something they valued, such as power or a title.
nuance.usage_note: In American business news, companies "divest" subsidiaries, assets or stock holdings, and investors "divest" from industries, such as fossil fuels, for ethical reasons. In everyday speech Americans more often say "get rid of" or "sell off"; "divest" is typical in formal or financial contexts. The most common phrase is "divest from" or "divest of."

distinctions.note: Invest means to put money or effort into something; divest is the opposite, to withdraw money or resources from it.
Sell is a general everyday word for exchanging something for money; divest suggests a deliberate, often strategic or ethical, withdrawal, often of a large holding or business unit.

examples.everyday: My uncle decided to divest from his old tech stocks and move the money into index funds.
examples.professional: The board voted to divest the logistics subsidiary before the end of the fiscal year.
examples.analytical: The reform aims to divest the institution of its historical privileges without dismantling its core mission.

nuance.analogy: Think of divest as emptying a backpack: you take out certain items and hand them over until nothing of that kind is left inside.
nuance.etymology: From Latin dis- (apart, away) plus vestire (to clothe), literally "to undress."
common_mistakes: Saying "divest the stock" when you mean sell, which sounds stiff in casual talk.
Using "divest" with "to" instead of "from" (say "divest from," not "divest to").
Stressing the first syllable (DI-vest) instead of the second.

divest.etymology: Alteration of *devest*, from Middle French *devester* (“strip of possessions”), from Old French *desvestir*, from *des-* (“dis-”) + *vestir* (“to clothe”).

senses.definition: To split or separate (something) into two or more parts.
senses.example: a wall divides two houses; a stream divides the towns

senses.definition: To separate into two or more parts.
To share (something) by dividing it.
senses.example: How shall we divide this pie?

senses.definition: To cause (a group of people) to disagree.
senses.example: Words divide us; Wiktionary unites us.

senses.definition: To calculate the quotient number by which another one (the divisor) is multiplied to produce a second number (the dividend).
senses.example: If you divide 6 by 3, you get 2.

senses.definition: To be a divisor of.
senses.example: 3 divides 6.

senses.definition: To reproduce by either mitosis or meiosis.
senses.example: Bacteria divide every twenty minutes under ideal laboratory conditions, doubling their population again and again.

senses.definition: To disunite in opinion or interest; to make discordant or hostile; to set at variance.
senses.example: The controversial zoning proposal began to divide the neighborhood, with families split against each other.

senses.definition: To vote, as in the British parliament and other legislatures, by the members separating themselves into two parties (as on opposite sides of the hall or in opposite lobbies), that is, the ayes dividing from the nays.
senses.example: After a long debate, the House voted, with members walking to opposite sides of the chamber to divide.

senses.definition: To split (something) into regular steps or intervals; to mark with degrees; to graduate.
senses.example: to divide a sextant

senses.definition: To play or sing in a florid style, or with variations.
senses.example: The jazz singer would divide each chorus into rapid, florid runs that delighted the audience.

senses.definition: A thing that divides.
senses.example: Stay on your side of the divide, please.

senses.definition: An act of dividing.
senses.example: The divide left most of the good land on my share of the property.

senses.definition: A distancing between two people or things.
senses.example: There is a great divide between us.

senses.definition: A large chasm, gorge, or ravine between two areas of land.
senses.example: If you're heading to the coast, you'll have to cross the divide first.

senses.definition: The topographical boundary dividing two adjacent catchment basins, such as a ridge or a crest.
senses.example: From the summit, we followed the continental divide, a narrow ridge separating rivers that flow east and west.

core.definition: To separate something into two or more parts, or to split a whole into shares.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable. The first vowel is a reduced 'dih', not 'dee', and the final -ide is a clear diphthong like 'hide'. Don't pronounce the final d as a separate sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in ordinary use, such as dividing food or tasks. It becomes negative when used about people, as in a divided nation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use divide constantly for food, money, chores, and work, such as 'let's divide the bill' or 'divide up the chores'. For a restaurant check, 'split the check' is more common and casual. Divide is also used figuratively for dividing groups of people, which can sound heavy in political contexts.

distinctions.note: Split is more casual and usually implies two parts; divide is more neutral and works for any number of parts.
Share focuses on giving portions to others, while divide focuses on the act of breaking the whole into pieces.

examples.everyday: Let's divide the pizza into eight slices so everyone gets one.
examples.professional: I'll divide the project into three phases so each team owns one deliverable.
examples.analytical: Kant divides human knowledge into analytic and synthetic judgments, and that distinction shapes his whole epistemology.

nuance.analogy: Like a cake sliced with a knife: the whole stays the same, but it now exists as separate pieces.
nuance.etymology: From Latin dividere, to force apart or separate, from dis- (apart) and a root for distribution.
common_mistakes: Using divide between with three or more people; use divide among for groups.
Saying 'divide to' someone instead of 'divide among' or 'divide between'.
Pronouncing the final vowel as 'dih-VEE-dih' rather than the single diphthong 'dih-VIDE'.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture divide often means to separate things that belong apart. In Genesis 1 God divides light from darkness and the waters from the waters, which is the Hebrew badal (to separate). The Greek merizo (to divide, apportion) appears when a man asks Jesus to tell his brother to divide an inheritance. Key passages: Genesis 1:4 describes God separating light from darkness; Exodus 14:21 describes the waters being divided so Israel could cross the sea; Luke 12:13-14 records the request about dividing an inheritance and Jesus refusing to act as judge.

divide.etymology: From Middle English *dividen*, from Latin *dīvidō* (“to divide”).

do-you-have-this-in-a-medium.phonetic: /du ju hæv ðɪs ɪn ə ˈmidiəm/

senses.definition: Asking whether the item comes in another size.

core.definition: Asking whether a clothing item is available in a medium size, the middle size between small and large.

pronunciation.respelling: doo yoo hav dhis in uh MEE-dee-um
pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable of 'medium' (MEE-dee-um), not the second. In fast speech 'you' becomes 'yuh' and 'a' becomes 'uh', so the whole question sounds like one smooth phrase.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a polite, ordinary request that shop staff hear all day, and it carries no pressure.
nuance.usage_note: Americans ask this at the fitting room, on the sales floor, or by calling a store. You can also say 'Do you have this in a medium?' while holding a shirt up to show which size you mean. A natural reply is 'Let me check' or 'Yes, I'll grab one for you'. In the US, 'medium' is the usual word; the sizes are often written S, M, L and XL.

distinctions.vs: Do you have a bigger one?
distinctions.note: Asks for a larger size without naming one, which is useful when you do not know your exact size.

distinctions.vs: Do you have this in a size medium?
distinctions.note: Also natural and common in American stores; 'in a size medium' is slightly more formal and emphasizes the size label.

examples.everyday: Hey, do you have this shirt in a medium? It looks like my size.
examples.professional: Before we order the company polos, do you have the navy version in a medium so I can check the fit?
examples.analytical: A size chart reports a single medium measurement, but a medium garment in one brand may fit like a small in another.

nuance.analogy: Like the middle setting on a thermostat: not the coldest or the hottest, but the one that fits most people.
nuance.etymology: Medium comes from Latin medius, meaning 'middle'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable as 'meh-DEE-um' instead of 'MEE-dee-um'.
Saying 'Do you have this in medium size?' with the article omitted; it is natural in speech, but 'in a medium' is the standard phrasing.

conversation.text: Excuse me, do you have this in a medium? I only see smalls.
This is a little snug. Do you have this in a medium?
I asked the clerk, "Do you have this in a medium?" and she checked the back.

senses.definition: Usually preceded by the: a state of apathy or lack of interest; a situation where one feels boredom, ennui, or tedium; a state of listlessness or malaise.
senses.example: I was in the doldrums yesterday and just didn’t feel inspired.

senses.definition: Usually preceded by the: the state of a sailing ship when it is impeded by calms or light, baffling winds, and is unable to make progress.
senses.example: The sailboat drifted for three days in the doldrums, waiting for any breath of wind.

senses.definition: Usually preceded by the: a part of the ocean near the equator where calms, squalls, and light, baffling winds are common.
senses.example: Sailors have long feared the doldrums near the equator, where winds die without warning.

core.definition: A state of low spirits, boredom or inactivity, when nothing seems to be moving forward or going well.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The -ums ending is pronounced like 'umz' with a weak vowel, and the r is clearly American.

nuance.connotation: Negative but mild. It describes a temporary slump rather than deep sadness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'the doldrums' for a slow period in business, sports, a relationship or one's mood. It is almost always used with 'the' and rarely in the singular. You might say 'the stock market is in the doldrums' or 'I've been in the doldrums since winter.' A natural reply is a sympathetic 'Hope it picks up soon.'

distinctions.note: Depression is a clinical or deep state of sadness, while the doldrums is a milder, often temporary slump.
A slump is a sudden drop in performance, while the doldrums suggests a longer period of stagnation or low energy.

examples.everyday: I've been in the doldrums all week, so let's go get some coffee and cheer up.
examples.professional: Sales have been in the doldrums since the second quarter, so we need a new plan.
examples.analytical: The essay describes a collective doldrums in which public enthusiasm has stagnated without a clear cause.

nuance.analogy: Like a sailboat stuck in a windless patch, your mood or business goes nowhere until a breeze comes up.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; probably connected with dull, first recorded in the 1700s in sailors' slang.
common_mistakes: Using 'a doldrums' or 'doldrum' as a common countable noun in everyday speech
Confusing it with 'the dumps', which is more informal

senses.definition: A substance, usually a liquid, used to clean drains by unclogging material lodged inside them.

core.definition: A product, usually a liquid chemical, used to clear clogs from sink, tub and shower drains by dissolving the material blocking them.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second word, CLEAN-er, more strongly than the first. The word 'drain' rhymes with 'rain,' and 'cleaner' ends in a clear American r-colored vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, with a safety warning; the product is useful but can be dangerous if misused.
nuance.usage_note: Americans buy drain cleaner at hardware stores and supermarkets, often for slow sinks or bathtubs. Strong chemical versions can burn skin and damage pipes, so the label should always be followed carefully. Americans also use plungers or drain snakes for clogs, which are non-chemical tools.

distinctions.note: A plunger is a rubber tool that uses pressure to clear a clog; drain cleaner is a chemical product that dissolves the material.
A drain snake, or auger, is a flexible metal cable used to break up or pull out clogs; drain cleaner works chemically.

collocations: clear a clog with drain cleaner
keep drain cleaner away from kids

examples.everyday: I poured some drain cleaner down the bathroom sink, but the water is still slow.
examples.professional: Facilities asked us not to use drain cleaner in the break room because it can corrode the old pipes.
examples.analytical: Chemical drain cleaners clear clogs by dissolving organic material, but they may damage the very pipes they are meant to protect.

nuance.analogy: Like a chemical snowplow clearing a blocked road inside the pipe.
nuance.etymology: A compound of drain and cleaner; drain traces to Old English drēahnian, 'to drain or dry out.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'drain cleaner' with equal stress on both words; the second word carries the main stress.
Mixing drain cleaner with other chemicals, which can create dangerous fumes; the label warns against it.

senses.definition: A sustained rebuke or censure.
senses.example: He received a severe dressing down from the head teacher.

core.definition: A severe scolding or rebuke, usually given sharply by a boss, parent, or other authority figure.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on DRESS, and down has secondary stress. Don't stress the -ing; it is a short, reduced vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes an unpleasant experience of being criticized harshly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'get a dressing down' or 'give someone a dressing down', usually about a serious mistake at work or at home. It is informal but not rude, and it implies anger more than calm correction. The noun is not used for casual clothing; that meaning belongs to 'dress down'.

distinctions.note: A reprimand is formal and often official or written, while a dressing down is a spoken, angry rebuke.
A lecture is long and educational, while a dressing down is shorter and more emotional.
Tongue-lashing is more vivid and forceful, while dressing down is the more neutral everyday term.

examples.everyday: After I forgot to call my sister on her birthday, I got a real dressing down from my mom.
examples.professional: The manager gave the team a dressing down after the failed release.
examples.analytical: A public dressing down may correct behavior, but it often damages the trust that learning depends on.

nuance.analogy: A dressing down is like a sudden storm of words that leaves you soaked and embarrassed.
nuance.etymology: From the verb dress down, 'to scold', with the -ing noun ending.
common_mistakes: Using 'dressing down' to mean casual clothing; that meaning belongs to 'dress down' or 'dress-down'.
Writing 'dressing-down' as a verb; the verb is 'dress down'.

senses.definition: Exhausting, menial, and tedious work.
senses.example: Sorting ten thousand paper invoices was pure drudgery, and she hated every minute of it.

core.definition: Hard, boring, repetitive work that is tiring and seems unimportant or unpleasant.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle syllable is a reduced schwa. The r is clear, and the final syllable is a light "ree" in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes unpleasant tasks that drain energy and offer little satisfaction.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use drudgery in everyday talk about chores, paperwork, or routine tasks, as in "the drudgery of commuting." It sounds a little literary, so people often use it in writing or in reflective speech. Casually, people may say grind or grunt work.

distinctions.note: A chore is a specific task you must do, while drudgery describes the tiring, monotonous nature of work as a whole.
Grind is more informal and often describes a hard routine, while drudgery is more formal and suggests dullness.

examples.everyday: Doing taxes by hand is pure drudgery, so I'm glad I finally bought software.
examples.professional: Automating the monthly reconciliation removes a lot of drudgery from the finance team's week.
examples.analytical: Aristotle distinguished the life of leisure from the drudgery of necessary labor.

nuance.analogy: Drudgery is like a long, flat road with no scenery, where each step is the same and you only want to reach the end.
nuance.etymology: From drudge, with the suffix -ery, from a Middle English word for servile work.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle vowel too strongly, as in "DRUJ-ah-REE."
Using drudgery as a countable noun, for example "a drudgery"; it is usually uncountable.

senses.definition: The male ruler of a duchy (female equivalent: duchess).
The sovereign of a small state.
A high title of nobility; the male holder of a dukedom.
A grand duke.
Any of various nymphalid butterflies of the Asian genera Bassarona and Dophla.
A fist.
senses.example: Put up your dukes!

senses.definition: To hit or beat with the fists.
To give cash to; to give a tip to.
senses.example: I duked him twenty dollars.

senses.definition: To perform the duties of, or rule over as, a duke.

core.definition: A man of the highest rank of nobility below royalty, who rules a duchy or holds a dukedom.

pronunciation.tip: Use a long oo sound and end with a clear, unreleased k. Avoid adding a y sound, which would make it sound like dyook.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans know duke mainly from royal news, historical novels and names such as Duke University or Duke Ellington. In everyday American speech, the verb phrase duke it out is common and informal, meaning to fight physically or argue hard until one side wins. The noble title itself is rarely used outside formal or historical contexts.

distinctions.note: An earl ranks below a duke and marquess in the British peerage, so a duke is the higher rank.
Duchess is the wife of a duke or a woman who holds a dukedom in her own right.

examples.everyday: Did you catch the royal news? A young duke just got married in London.
examples.professional: The foundation's honorary board includes a duke who has supported the arts for decades.
examples.analytical: Medieval dukes often controlled territories that rivaled royal power, which is why monarchs guarded the title carefully.

nuance.analogy: Like a regional governor under a king, a duke ruled a large territory on the monarch's behalf.
nuance.etymology: From Latin dux, leader, through Old French duc.
common_mistakes: Confusing duke with duck or dook in pronunciation.
Using duke for any noble; it is a specific high rank, not a general word for a lord.

duke.etymology: From Old French *duc*, through Middle English *duk*, *duke*, from Latin *dux*.

senses.definition: A heap of dung, especially one for agricultural purposes.
senses.example: The farmer hauled wheelbarrows of manure to the dunghill behind the barn each morning.

senses.definition: Any wretchedly mean, dirty or loathsome place, situation or condition.
senses.example: The rented room was a dunghill of stale food, dirty laundry, and broken furniture.

core.definition: A heap of animal manure or waste; also, any very dirty or unpleasant place.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and keep the ng sound from dung. The final syllable is a short hil, like hill without the extra sound.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative, expressing disgust or contempt.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use dunghill in daily life; it appears mainly in older literature, older translations of the Bible, or dramatic speech. Everyday American speakers would say manure pile or compost heap for the literal meaning. Calling a place a dunghill is an old-fashioned insult that can sound theatrical today.

distinctions.note: Manure pile is the plain, modern American term for the literal heap of waste; dunghill is older and often figurative.
An ash heap is a pile of burned waste or cinders; dunghill specifically suggests animal waste and stronger disgust.

examples.everyday: The old barn turned into a dunghill after the animals were kept there all summer.
examples.professional: The facilities team said the loading area had become a dunghill of spoiled material.
examples.analytical: In Scripture, the dunghill often stands for humiliation, a contrast with the honor God gives to the poor.

nuance.analogy: A dunghill is like a trash pile for the soul: it stands for the lowest, most degraded place a person can be.
nuance.etymology: From dung and hill, literally a hill of dung.
common_mistakes: Using dunghill casually in everyday speech, where it sounds dramatic or archaic.
Spelling it as dung hill with two words; the standard form is one word.
nuance.biblical_note: Dunghill appears in older English Bibles, such as the King James Version, to render Hebrew words for ash heap or refuse pile. In the Revised Standard Version, the same images are often rendered as ash heap, as in 1 Samuel 2:8 and Psalm 113:7, where God lifts the poor from the ash heap. The image expresses God's reversal of fortunes, lifting the humble and lowly from shame. Lamentations 4:5 also uses a related image of people who once lived in luxury now lying in the ash heap.

senses.definition: The receding movement of the tide.
senses.example: The boats will go out on the ebb.

senses.definition: A gradual decline.
A low state; a state of depression.
senses.example: Her confidence reached an ebb after the third rejected grant application.

senses.definition: A European bunting, the corn bunting (Emberiza calandra, syns. Emberiza miliaria, Milaria calandra).
Low, shallow.
senses.example: The ebb water along the sandbar was so shallow that we could see the ripples.

senses.definition: To flow back or recede.
senses.example: The tides ebbed at noon.

senses.definition: To fall away or decline.
senses.example: The dying man's strength ebbed away.

senses.definition: To fish with stakes and nets that serve to prevent the fish from getting back into the sea with the ebb.
senses.example: Fishermen on the Bay of Fundy once ebbed their nets to trap fish returning to the sea.

senses.definition: To cause to flow back.
senses.example: The dam gates ebb the river's flow back upstream during maintenance.

core.definition: The movement of the tide back out to sea, or a gradual decline in strength or amount.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short e as in bed, and end with a clear b. Do not stretch the vowel into ee or ay.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative, depending on whether it describes the tide or a decline. It often signals loss or decline in a sad or serious tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ebb most often in the phrase ebb and flow, which describes natural cycles, and in at a low ebb, which describes poor condition. In casual speech people more often say decline or go down, so ebb sounds more literary. For the tide, Americans usually say the tide is going out.

distinctions.note: Decline is a general word for becoming less, while ebb suggests a natural or temporary receding, often like a tide.
Flow is the opposite movement, flowing in or continuing, and it is used in the phrase ebb and flow.

examples.everyday: The beach was empty because the tide was at its ebb.
examples.professional: Our team morale is at a low ebb after the failed launch, so we need a clear plan.
examples.analytical: The author describes the ebb and flow of religious enthusiasm across centuries.

nuance.analogy: Like the sea pulling back from the shore, ebb describes something that slowly moves away before it may return.
nuance.etymology: Ebb comes from Old English ebba, meaning the outgoing tide.
common_mistakes: Confusing ebb with web or with eb pronounced with a long vowel.
Using ebb as a verb with an object, such as ebb the water, which is not standard.
patterns: the ebb and flow of sth

ebb.etymology: From Middle English *ebbe*, from Old English *ebba* (“ebb, tide”), from **abbjā*, from Proto-Germanic **abjô*, **abjǭ*, from Proto-Germanic **ab* (“off, away”), from Proto-Indo-European **apó*.

senses.definition: Feeling or characterized by ecstasy.
senses.example: The crowd was ecstatic when the band finally walked onstage after the delay.

senses.definition: Extremely happy.
Relating to, or caused by, ecstasy or excessive emotion.
senses.example: ecstatic gaze ecstatic trance

senses.definition: Transports of delight; words or actions performed in a state of ecstasy.
senses.example: The sermon moved from quiet prayer into wild ecstatics that shook the old wooden pews.

senses.definition: A person in a state of ecstasy.
senses.example: The fervent ecstatic in the front row swayed and sang long after the hymn ended.

core.definition: Extremely happy or excited; overjoyed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the middle syllable, STAT. The final syllable is short, "ik", not "ick" with a long vowel, and the "c" is hard like "k".

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests strong, happy excitement, and it can be used lightly or dramatically.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ecstatic casually to describe excited happiness about news, results, or a gift, as in "I was ecstatic when I got the job." It is also used in reviews, sports, and news reports. It is strong, so don't use it for mild satisfaction.

distinctions.note: Happy is the general word; ecstatic is much stronger and suggests overwhelming excitement.
Thrilled is common and warm; ecstatic is a bit stronger and more dramatic.

examples.everyday: My sister was ecstatic when she got into her first-choice college.
examples.professional: The client was ecstatic about the results and asked us to expand the pilot.
examples.analytical: In William James's account, ecstatic experience often exceeds the reach of ordinary language.

nuance.analogy: Being ecstatic is like a kid on the last day of school: the joy fills the whole body.
nuance.etymology: From Greek ekstatikos, "driven out of one's senses", from ekstasis.
common_mistakes: Using "ecstatic" for mild happiness, which sounds exaggerated.
Pronouncing the stress on the last syllable, as in "ek-STAT-ick" with a long vowel.

conversation.text: The fans were ecstatic when their team won the championship.
I was ecstatic when I heard I got the scholarship.
She'll be ecstatic when she sees the new puppy.

senses.definition: A state of being bright and radiant, splendor, brilliance.

core.definition: Bright, radiant light or brilliance, often used for splendor in a beautiful or spiritual sense.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on FUL, the second syllable. The -ence ending is a reduced 'uns', and the 'g' sounds like 'j' before the 'e'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests dazzling, almost sacred brightness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use effulgence in poetry, sermons, and descriptions of sunrises, stars, or glory. It is not a conversational word, so people would say 'brightness' or 'glow' in ordinary talk. The word is most natural in writing that wants a grand, elevated tone.

distinctions.note: Brightness is a neutral everyday word for light intensity; effulgence implies a splendid, almost overwhelming radiance.
Radiance is more common and can describe a person's glow; effulgence is more literary and grand.

examples.everyday: The sunrise over the lake had a golden effulgence that made us stop the car.
examples.professional: The presentation's visuals had a kind of effulgence, though the content underneath was thin.
examples.analytical: Medieval theologians often described divine goodness as an effulgence that spills out into creation.

nuance.analogy: Effulgence is like the light of a lamp turned up so high that the whole room glows.
nuance.etymology: From Latin effulgere, to shine forth, from ex- plus fulgere, to shine.
common_mistakes: Using effulgence in casual conversation, where it sounds overly grand.
Confusing effulgence with effluence, which means a flowing out.

effulgence.etymology: From Latin *ex-* (“out of, from”) and *fulgo* (“to shine”).

senses.definition: Complex, detailed, or sophisticated.
senses.example: After reading a long, elaborate description, I was impressed but no wiser.

senses.definition: Intricate, fancy, flashy, or showy.
senses.example: I stared for hours at the elaborate pattern in the rug.

senses.definition: Тo develop in detail or complexity.
senses.example: The architect asked the team to elaborate on the plan before approving the budget.

senses.definition: To expand/enlarge in detail.
senses.example: What do you mean you didn't come home last night? Would you care to elaborate?

core.definition: Complex, detailed, or sophisticated; in a showier sense, intricate, fancy, or flashy in design or decoration.

pronunciation.tip: The adjective is stressed on the first syllable of the middle, 'LAB', and ends in a reduced 'uht'. The verb is pronounced differently, ending in 'rate' (ih-LAB-uh-rayt), so do not use the verb ending for the adjective.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when describing careful work; negative when it implies unnecessary complexity or showiness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'elaborate' for detailed plans, meals, costumes, or systems. It can praise careful work or criticize something as needlessly complicated, depending on tone. In everyday talk, 'complicated' or 'fancy' is often more natural for things that are only a bit intricate. Saying 'an elaborate plan' is common in both work and casual settings.

distinctions.note: Complicated stresses difficulty for the person, while elaborate stresses many carefully arranged parts, which may be impressive.
Detailed describes a level of specific information. Elaborate adds the sense of intricacy or design and often a showy quality.

examples.everyday: My sister threw an elaborate birthday party with a balloon arch and a cake shaped like a castle.
examples.professional: The team's data pipeline is elaborate, with a dozen transformation steps that nobody on the current team fully understands.
examples.analytical: Scholastic arguments are often elaborate, not because the truth is complicated, but because each distinction must be defended against objections.

nuance.analogy: Like a wedding cake with layers of sugar roses, an elaborate design has many carefully arranged parts.
nuance.etymology: From Latin elaboratus, past participle of elaborare ('to work out'), from e- and labor ('work').
common_mistakes: Using the verb pronunciation (ih-LAB-uh-rayt) for the adjective.
Forgetting the preposition with the verb: say 'elaborate on the point', not 'elaborate the point' in the sense of explaining further.

elaborate.etymology: 1575, from Late Latin *ēlabōrātus* (“worked out”), past participle of *ēlabōrō* (“to work out”), from *ē-* (“out, forth, fully”) + *labor* (“work, toil, exertion”).

senses.definition: Related to electricity (or electronics)
senses.example: electrical engineering for the design of electrical appliances

senses.definition: An electrical engineer.
senses.example: My cousin is an electrical who designs wiring for hospitals across the state.

core.definition: Relating to electricity, or to the equipment, wiring, and systems that use electricity.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and reduce the final -ical to a light uh-l sound. Do not pronounce the k as a hard ch-like sound, and keep the r clear in General American.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, technical, and practical.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use electrical for wiring, outlets, systems, and fields of study, such as electrical wiring, an electrical outlet, or electrical engineering. In everyday speech, a plain electrical problem usually means something wrong with the wires or fuse box. Electric is used more for devices that run on power.

distinctions.note: Electrical describes systems and fields connected with electricity, while electric describes devices that run on it.
Electronic refers to circuits with active components such as transistors, while electrical is broader and includes wiring and power.

examples.everyday: Don't touch that cord, because there's an electrical problem in the wall behind the couch.
examples.professional: Our electrical team needs to inspect the panel before the city inspector comes on Friday.
examples.analytical: The electrical model of the nervous system treats neurons as circuits, though that metaphor simplifies chemical signaling.

nuance.analogy: Electrical is like plumbing for power: it describes the pipes and fittings, not just the water.
nuance.etymology: From electric, from New Latin electricus, 'of amber', with the adjective ending -al.
common_mistakes: Using electric where Americans normally say electrical, as in electric engineering.
Pronouncing it ee-LEK-trih-kal, which shifts the stress and vowel incorrectly.

senses.definition: The materialist view that the majority of the mental states assumed by common sense like belief or sensation do not exist.

core.definition: The philosophical view that common-sense mental states such as beliefs and sensations do not really exist and should be replaced by neuroscience.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LIM, and the -ive and -ism endings are unstressed. Many learners add an extra syllable after the m, so keep it as ih-LIM-in-uh-tiv-iz-um.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is a specialist term that can sound provocative in general conversation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use eliminativism mainly in academic philosophy, especially in philosophy of mind. It is a shorter name for eliminative materialism, and speakers in the field use the two terms interchangeably. In everyday talk you would explain the idea rather than use the word.

distinctions.note: Behaviorism explains mind in terms of observable behavior; eliminativism denies that common-sense mental states exist at all.
Reductionism says a higher-level thing can be explained by lower-level facts; eliminativism says the higher-level thing is not real.

examples.everyday: My brother is studying philosophy and told me he thinks eliminativism is probably true.
examples.professional: In the reading group, we compared eliminativism with more moderate views about how brain science relates to psychology.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that eliminativism is self-undermining, since the claim that beliefs do not exist seems to be a belief itself.

nuance.analogy: Like a mapmaker who says that a village on the old map never existed and should be erased, eliminativism removes the familiar categories of mind.
nuance.etymology: Formed in the late twentieth century from eliminate and -ism.
common_mistakes: Using eliminativism to mean the simple act of eliminating things, as in the elimination of options.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying ee-lih-MIN-uh-tiv-iz-um.

senses.definition: Supporting eliminativism, the materialist position which holds that folk psychology presents a false view of the mind.
senses.example: Her eliminativist account of the mind argues that everyday talk about beliefs and desires is misleading.

senses.definition: A supporter of eliminativism.
senses.example: As an eliminativist, he argued that folk psychology will eventually be replaced by neuroscience.

core.definition: Supporting eliminativism, the view that common-sense talk of beliefs and desires is a false theory that science will eventually discard.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LIM, the second syllable, and the -ative part is reduced to 'uh-tiv'. Say the final -ist clearly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical label, though it may sound provocative to dualists or believers in the mind.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use eliminativist mainly in philosophy of mind, cognitive science and academic debate. Calling someone an eliminativist is a precise label rather than an insult, but it can start an argument, so use it when you need precision. Many people say eliminative materialist when they want to be clearer.

distinctions.note: A reductive materialist says mental states are identical to brain states, while an eliminativist says mental states such as beliefs do not exist at all.
A dualist holds that mind and body are two different kinds of substance, while an eliminativist rejects the existence of mental states altogether.

examples.everyday: My roommate who studies neuroscience calls himself an eliminativist, which started a fight about whether he believes in his own feelings.
examples.professional: Our analysis should avoid eliminativist shortcuts, since the stakeholders still talk about user intentions in every meeting.
examples.analytical: An eliminativist must explain why belief talk succeeds in prediction even if beliefs turn out not to exist.

nuance.analogy: Like declaring that phlogiston does not exist and that chemists should drop the word, an eliminativist wants science to discard folk psychology.
nuance.etymology: From eliminate plus -ive and -ist; the philosophical sense comes from eliminative materialism, which Paul Churchland helped popularize in the 1980s.
common_mistakes: Using eliminativist as a loose synonym for skeptic; the word refers specifically to denying that mental states exist.
Confusing eliminativist with eliminationist, which means someone who wants to remove a group of people.

senses.definition: (rare) The act of eluding.
senses.example: Her elusion of the reporters frustrated the crowd waiting outside the courthouse.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: The act of escaping or avoiding something, such as a pursuer, a responsibility or a difficult question.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on LOO, and the 'si' sound is pronounced like the 'zh' in 'vision'. The final syllable is a reduced 'un'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; can imply deliberate avoidance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use elusion; they say evasion, escape or avoidance. In legal and political writing, evasion is the usual word, as in tax evasion. Elusion appears mostly in literary or scholarly writing, so in casual talk say he got away or he avoided it.

distinctions.note: Evasion is the common word and is often negative, as in tax evasion or evasion of a question; elusion is rarer and more literary.
Escape is a plain everyday word for getting free; elusion is an abstract noun for the act of slipping away, usually in writing.

examples.everyday: Grandpa always tells the story of his elusion of the bear, though nobody believes the bear part.
examples.professional: The memo describes a pattern of elusion, where managers avoided direct questions about the delayed release.
examples.analytical: The author's elusion of the central question makes the essay feel polished but empty.

nuance.analogy: Like an eel slipping out of a fisherman's grip.
nuance.etymology: From elude, from Latin eludere, to escape by playing, from e- (away) and ludere (to play).
common_mistakes: Confusing elusion with illusion, which means a false appearance or belief.
Pronouncing the s as a plain s sound; it is pronounced like zh, as in 'vision'.

senses.definition: In an empathetic way.
senses.example: She listened empathetically to her coworker's story about losing her father.

core.definition: In a way that shows you understand and share another person's feelings, and want to help or support them.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on THEH, the third syllable, with a lighter stress on EM. The th is voiceless, as in 'think', and the -ly ending is 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes warm, caring understanding, and it is often used to praise how someone listened or responded.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use empathetically in formal writing, counseling, healthcare, and customer service reports. In everyday speech they more often say 'I totally get it' or 'that sounds really hard', and they describe the action without the adverb. The adjective empathetic is much more common than the adverb.

distinctions.note: Sympathetically means feeling sorry for someone or showing agreement, often from the outside, while empathetically means sharing their feelings from the inside.
Empathically is an accepted variant, but empathetically is more common in American writing; both mean the same.
Compassionately focuses on the wish to relieve suffering, while empathetically focuses on understanding the other person's feelings.

examples.everyday: When I told my neighbor about my dad's surgery, she listened empathetically and asked how I was holding up.
examples.professional: Our support team is trained to respond empathetically when a customer is frustrated, before offering a fix.
examples.analytical: The author writes empathetically about the soldier's guilt, so the reader is led to share his moral confusion rather than judge it.

nuance.analogy: Like standing in someone's shoes and noticing exactly where they pinch.
nuance.etymology: From Greek empatheia, meaning 'passion' or 'affection', from en (in) and pathos (feeling).
common_mistakes: Confusing empathetically (sharing feelings) with sympathetically (feeling sorry for someone).
Stressing the first syllable in the wrong place; the main stress belongs on THEH.

senses.definition: To carry a sentence over to the next line without a pause.

core.definition: In poetry, to continue a sentence past the end of a line without a pause, running it into the next line.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, JAM, and the j sounds like the j in jam. The word ends in an m sound, so do not add a b; it looks like the word jamb, a door frame.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: a technical term in poetry analysis.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use enjamb mainly in poetry classes, literary criticism and writing about verse forms. You will rarely hear it in ordinary conversation. Use it when describing how a poet breaks a line in the middle of a sentence, as in blank verse.

distinctions.note: An end-stopped line ends with punctuation or a full grammatical pause; enjambment is the opposite, carrying the sentence over to the next line.
A caesura is a pause within a line; enjambment is a phrase carried over the end of a line, so the two can occur in the same poem.

examples.professional: For the workshop, we marked where each poem enjambs and where it pauses.
examples.analytical: Milton often enjambs his blank verse, letting the syntax carry the reader across the line break.

nuance.analogy: Like a river that does not stop at a bridge: the sentence flows over the line break and into the next one.
nuance.etymology: From French enjamber 'to straddle or stride over', from en- plus jambe 'leg'.
common_mistakes: Confusing enjamb with enjoy or with jamb; the stress is on the second syllable, en-JAM.
Using enjamb for any line break; it specifically means a sentence running on without a pause.

senses.definition: The act of logically entailing, the state of being entailed, or something that is entailed.
senses.example: Entailment does not imply causation: if a set of premisses entail a conclusion, that does not mean (necessarily) that they cause that conclusion to be true.

senses.definition: The act of setting up an entail to restrict inheritance.
senses.example: The lawyer's entailment of the estate ensured it passed only to direct male heirs.

core.definition: In logic, the relation in which the truth of one statement necessarily guarantees the truth of another statement.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on -TAYL-, and the final -ment is a reduced syllable, so say munt. Do not separate the l and the m into two syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is precise and used without any emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use entailment in logic, philosophy, linguistics, and some legal writing, usually in a classroom, paper, or technical discussion. In everyday speech it would sound overly academic. When explaining the idea casually, people say if one thing is true, the other must be true.

distinctions.note: Implication is a broader and looser term in ordinary speech, while entailment is a strict logical relation where the conclusion must follow.
Inference is the act of drawing a conclusion, while entailment is the relation that makes the conclusion follow necessarily.

examples.everyday: My philosophy class got into a debate about whether saying he is a bachelor entailment that he is unmarried.
examples.professional: The NLP team evaluates the model on textual entailment, checking whether a hypothesis follows from the premise.
examples.analytical: Tarski's definition of logical consequence treats entailment as a relation holding in virtue of the logical form of the sentences involved.

nuance.analogy: Entailment is like a row of dominoes: once the first one falls, the next must fall too, with no way to stop the chain.
nuance.etymology: From entail (verb) plus the suffix -ment, meaning the result or state of entailing.
common_mistakes: Using entailment as a casual word for hint; in logic it means necessary consequence.
Confusing the noun entailment with the verb entail when a sentence needs a verb.

senses.definition: With zealous fervor; excited, motivated.
senses.example: an enthusiastic lover of art

senses.definition: Relating to enthusiasm, or divine possession.
senses.example: The preacher's enthusiastic sermon described the spirit descending upon the congregation like fire.

core.definition: Showing great excitement, eagerness and energy about something you like or want to do.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on the -as- syllable, and the -ic ending is /ɪk/. Many learners stress the -thu- or -zi- parts, or add an extra syllable, so keep the stress on AS and say the ending short.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it signals sincere eagerness, though an overly eager tone can sound naive or, in some contexts, slightly sarcastic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use enthusiastic in everyday talk and at work: 'We're enthusiastic about the new project.' To accept an invitation, you can say 'Yes, enthusiastically!' or more casually 'Count me in'. Be careful with the tone: 'Oh, how enthusiastic!' can be sarcastic, especially when someone is clearly unhappy about a task.

distinctions.note: Keen is more understated and is often followed by 'on' or 'to', while enthusiastic describes a more open, energetic display.
Eager stresses a desire to act soon, while enthusiastic stresses energy and excitement about the activity or idea.
Passionate suggests deep, strong emotion, often about beliefs or love, while enthusiastic is more outward, cheerful and energetic.

examples.everyday: My son is enthusiastic about the soccer team, and he never misses a practice.
examples.professional: The client gave an enthusiastic response to the prototype, so we moved on to the next phase.
examples.analytical: Enthusiastic religious movements often raise the question of whether emotional fervor is evidence of truth or only its expression.

nuance.analogy: Like a dog hearing its owner's car keys: the whole body moves forward at once.
nuance.etymology: From Greek enthousiasmos, 'divine inspiration, possession by a god', from enthousios, 'inspired, possessed by a god'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'he is an enthusiastic' instead of 'he is an enthusiast' when referring to a person who loves a hobby.
Using the wrong preposition; say enthusiastic about, not enthusiastic of or for.

enthusiastic.etymology: From Ancient Greek *ἐνθουσιαστικός*, from either *ἐνθουσιασμός* or *ἐνθουσιάζω* + *-τικός*.

senses.definition: The art or science of innovation and risk-taking for profit in business.
The quality of being an entrepreneur.

core.definition: The activity of starting and running a new business, including the creativity and financial risk involved in pursuing profit.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the 'nur' syllable, and make the ending '-ship' short and unstressed, like 'ship' with a reduced vowel. The 'eur' spelling is pronounced as the vowel in 'burn'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. In American culture it is strongly admired and is often used in praise of new business creation, in schools, universities and government programs.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use entrepreneurship in business schools, startup communities, government programs and news about small business. It is a formal-to-neutral word, so it is natural in a class, a presentation or a discussion of the economy. In casual talk, people more often say 'starting a business' or 'going out on your own'.

distinctions.note: An entrepreneur is a person, while entrepreneurship is the activity or quality of doing that work.
Enterprise means a business or organization, and can also mean a bold undertaking; entrepreneurship refers to the act or practice of creating such ventures.

examples.everyday: My neighbor took a night class in entrepreneurship and then quit his job to open a bakery.
examples.professional: Our entrepreneurship program at work gives employees small budgets to test new product ideas.
examples.analytical: Entrepreneurship is often praised as a driver of innovation, but its economic benefits depend on institutions that distribute risk fairly.

nuance.analogy: Entrepreneurship is like sailing a boat you built yourself: you choose the course and carry the risk, and you also keep whatever you catch.
nuance.etymology: From entrepreneur plus the suffix -ship, meaning state or quality of; entrepreneur comes from French, from entreprendre, to undertake.
common_mistakes: Spelling entrepreneurship with -ur- and -eur- confused, especially writing 'entrepenuership'.
Using entrepreneurship to mean only owning a business, when it refers to the process of creating and developing one.

senses.definition: To remove hair from the skin in such a way that removes or destroys the root, especially by plucking it out.
senses.example: She chose to epilate her eyebrows with tweezers and a steady hand each morning.

core.definition: To remove unwanted hair by pulling it out from the root, usually with an electric device, so that it grows back more slowly.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, EP. The final syllable rhymes with 'late' and ends in a clear 't' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a beauty and personal care term, usually found on product labels.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'epilate' in everyday talk. They say 'wax', 'sugar', 'tweeze' or 'get laser hair removal', and the word appears mostly on product packaging or in beauty and medical contexts. Saying 'I epilated my legs' is understood but sounds a bit formal or clinical.

distinctions.note: Shaving cuts hair at the surface, so it grows back quickly; epilation removes hair from the root, so regrowth is slower.
Depilating removes hair at or near the surface without pulling out the root; epilating removes the root itself.
Waxing is the most common method and also removes hair from the root; 'epilate' is the general term for any root-removal method, while 'wax' names one specific technique.

examples.professional: The salon offers laser treatment as a longer-lasting alternative to epilating at home.
examples.analytical: The label claims the device epilates, which means it removes hair from the root rather than merely cutting it at the surface.

nuance.analogy: Like pulling a weed up by its root instead of mowing the top, so it takes longer to come back.
nuance.etymology: From Latin e- 'out' and pilus 'hair', in its modern cosmetic sense.
common_mistakes: Using 'epilate' to mean shaving, which only cuts the hair at the surface.
Confusing 'epilate' with 'depilate', which removes hair without pulling out the root.

senses.definition: Having the equipment, resources, and skills one needs; prepared.

core.definition: Having the tools, resources, skills, or knowledge needed to do something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the one syllable, KWIPT. The final -ed is silent and sounds like a 't', so say the 'p' and then 't' with no extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral; being 'well equipped' is a compliment, while being 'ill-equipped' signals a problem.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'equipped' in everyday talk about readiness, such as 'Are you equipped for this snow?' It often pairs with 'to' or 'for' for a task, or 'with' for objects. In casual talk, 'ready' or 'set up' can work too, but 'equipped' sounds more precise.

distinctions.note: Prepared means you have planned or trained in advance; equipped means you have the actual tools, skills, or resources.
Qualified implies official credentials or a formal standard; equipped refers to practical ability and resources.

examples.everyday: Are you equipped for this snow, or should we stop and get some boots first?
examples.professional: Our team is equipped with the tools to monitor model drift in production, so we can respond quickly.
examples.analytical: A theory is only as strong as the concepts it is equipped to explain, and many frameworks are not equipped to handle anomalies at all.

nuance.analogy: Being equipped is like packing a backpack before a hike: the bag holds what you will need on the trail.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of 'equip', from French équiper, from Old Norse skipa, 'to man a ship'.
common_mistakes: Using 'equipped of' instead of 'equipped with'.
Confusing 'equipped to' and 'equipped for': say 'equipped to handle a problem' and 'equipped for a trip'.

senses.definition: Of sounds, especially speech: demonstrating or possessing euphony; agreeable to the ear; pleasant-sounding.

core.definition: Pleasant to hear; having a smooth, agreeable sound, especially in speech, music or the sound of words.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on FOH, the second syllable. Keep the final -ous unstressed, sounding like 'us', and do not say 'yoo-fon-ee-OUS.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises a sound, most often a voice, a name or a phrase.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this adjective in literary criticism, music reviews, or when praising a speaker's voice or a well-sounding name. In everyday talk they would more often say 'pretty,' 'nice to listen to' or 'musical.' Using it in casual conversation can sound showy.

distinctions.note: Melodious refers to a tune or melody; euphonious refers to the pleasing sound of speech or words.
Harmonious means in agreement or in balanced parts; euphonious refers only to pleasing sound.

examples.everyday: Her name is so euphonious that people always remember it.
examples.professional: The brand team chose a euphonious product name that is easy to say in both English and Spanish.
examples.analytical: Poe argued that a euphonious line gains its power from the repeated long vowels that carry the emotion of the poem.

nuance.analogy: Like a well-tuned bell: each word rings clearly and pleasantly.
nuance.etymology: From Greek euphōnos, 'sweet-sounding,' from eu- 'well' and phōnē 'sound, voice.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, saying 'yoo-FON-ee-us.'
Using it for pleasant things in general rather than for sound.

senses.definition: To draw conclusions from examining; to assess; to appraise.
senses.example: It will take several years to evaluate the material gathered in the survey.

senses.definition: To compute or determine the value of (an expression).
senses.example: Evaluate this integral.

senses.definition: To return or have a specific value.
senses.example: The function will evaluate to true whenever the input list is empty.

core.definition: To judge the quality, worth, or effectiveness of something by examining it carefully and forming a conclusion about it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable VAL, and the middle syllable is weak, so say 'ih-VAL-yoo-ayt' rather than 'ee-val-oo-ATE'. Keep the 'yoo' sound short and unstressed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds objective and careful, and it implies a considered judgment rather than a quick opinion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use evaluate constantly at work, in schools, and in healthcare, for things like evaluating a candidate, a program, or a patient. In casual talk people often say 'check it out', 'look at it', or 'see how it went' instead. Evaluate is standard in meetings and written reports.

distinctions.note: Assess is broader and often implies estimating level or need, while evaluate usually implies a more formal judgment against criteria.
Judge is more personal and can be casual or moral, while evaluate sounds systematic and professional.
Review means to look at again or formally examine, and it is often used for a document or a performance cycle; evaluate stresses the final judgment.

examples.everyday: Before we buy the couch, let's evaluate whether it'll fit through the door.
examples.professional: Can you evaluate the three vendor proposals and send me your recommendation by Friday?
examples.analytical: Any ethical theory must be able to evaluate actions against a standard that is not simply the agent's own preference.

nuance.analogy: Like a referee checking a replay: they look at the evidence closely before deciding what it means.
nuance.etymology: From French évaluer, from é- (out) and value, from Latin valere (to be worth).
common_mistakes: Saying 'evaluate about' instead of 'evaluate' directly, as in 'evaluate the options', not 'evaluate about the options'.
Stressing the last syllable as 'ee-val-oo-ATE'; the stress belongs on VAL.

senses.definition: Although; though; despite or in spite of the fact that.
senses.example: She left him even though she still loved him.

core.definition: Although; despite the fact that something is true. Introduces a contrast with the main clause.

pronunciation.tip: Stress EE in even. Though is weak in the phrase and usually says thoh, but it is not a stressed word. Do not say even tho or even dough.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It presents a contrast without judgment and works in speech and writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use even though in everyday speech and in writing to show a fact that does not stop the main action: 'I went out even though I was tired.' It is a little stronger than although. Do not add but after the main clause, as in 'Even though it rained, but we went.' A natural reply is 'Yeah, I know, but thanks for coming.'

distinctions.note: Although is slightly more formal and can appear more often in written prose. Even though adds more emphasis on the contrast and is common in speech.
Even if introduces a hypothetical or uncertain condition. Even though introduces a fact that is already true.

examples.everyday: Let's go for a walk, even though it's kind of cold out.
examples.professional: We shipped the release on time even though QA had found two open bugs.
examples.analytical: Even though the correlation is strong, we cannot infer causation from observational data alone.

nuance.analogy: Like a runner who keeps going despite a stitch in her side.
nuance.etymology: Even (adverb, emphasizing) combined with though, from Old English thah.
common_mistakes: Adding but after the main clause, as in 'Even though it was late, but we went.'
Confusing even though with even if when the situation is a fact rather than a hypothesis.

senses.definition: Lasting or enduring forever; endless, eternal.
Chiefly of a deity or other supernatural being: having always existed and will continue to exist forever; eternal.
senses.example: Many believers picture God as an everlasting being who never began and never ends.

senses.definition: Synonym of sempiternal (“having infinite temporal duration, rather than outside time and thus lacking temporal duration altogether”).
senses.example: Philosophers debated whether the universe is everlasting or had a definite beginning.

senses.definition: Continuing for a long period; eternal.
senses.example: this everlasting nonsense

senses.definition: Happening all the time, especially to a tiresome extent; constant, incessant, unending.
senses.example: I'm tired of your everlasting complaints about the parking situation at work.

senses.definition: Of clothing or fabric: lasting a long time; very durable or hard-wearing.
senses.example: These denim jeans are everlasting, and I've worn the same pair for five years.

senses.definition: Having flowers that retain their color and form when dried.
senses.example: The florist arranged everlasting blooms in a basket that would keep their color for years.

senses.definition: Of a plant or plant part: synonym of perennial (“active throughout the year, or having a life cycle of more than two growing seasons”).
senses.example: Yarrow is an everlasting herb that returns to my backyard garden every spring.

senses.definition: Used as an intensifier.
Chiefly in the name of a plant:
senses.example: Her garden was full of everlasting peas climbing the old wooden fence.

senses.definition: Synonym of everlastingly.
senses.example: The old preacher prayed everlasting for the lost souls of the town.

senses.definition: Used as an intensifier: extremely, very.
senses.example: It was everlasting hot in that kitchen all summer long.

senses.definition: In an everlasting (adjective sense 1) manner; forever.
senses.example: The lamp in the chapel would burn everlasting before the altar.

senses.definition: Chiefly with a descriptive word: short for everlasting flower (“any of several plants, chiefly of the family Asteraceae (principally the tribe Gnaphalieae), having flowers that retain their color and form when dried; also, a flower of such a plant”)
senses.example: She dried a bunch of everlasting from the garden for the hallway vase.

senses.definition: Synonym of lasting (“ a durable, plain, woven fabric formerly used for making clothes and for the uppers of women's shoes; a quantity of such fabric”).
senses.example: The tailor bought yards of everlasting to line the wool coat.

senses.definition: Short for everlasting trimming (“ an embroidered edging used on underclothes; a quantity of such edging”)
senses.example: Her grandmother sewed a strip of everlasting along the hem of the petticoat.

core.definition: Lasting forever, without end; used for things that seem never to stop or for God as eternal.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on LAS, and the first syllable has a light secondary stress. Americans pronounce the r in the middle, so say ev-er, not ev-uh, and keep the final ng sound.

nuance.connotation: Usually positive or reverent, meaning eternal or enduring. In casual speech it can be sarcastic, as in everlasting rain.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use everlasting in religious, poetic, and emotional contexts, and sometimes humorously for something that seems endless. In everyday conversation people more often say never-ending or forever. Using everlasting for a literal, practical duration sounds odd.

distinctions.note: Eternal has a theological or philosophical weight and suggests no beginning or end, while everlasting stresses endless duration.
Lasting means durable for a long time, while everlasting means it will never end.

examples.everyday: My grandmother always said her cooking was not everlasting, but it made the whole house feel warm.
examples.professional: The vendor promised everlasting uptime, which is impossible, so we need a realistic service level.
examples.analytical: Scripture speaks of everlasting covenant, and theologians debate how it relates to temporal history.

nuance.analogy: Everlasting is like a flame that never goes out, no matter how long you watch it.
nuance.etymology: From ever plus lasting, from Old English roots for always and continue.
common_mistakes: Using everlasting for ordinary durability, as in this battery is everlasting; say this battery lasts a long time.
Confusing everlasting with everlastingly, the adverb; use everlastingly for the manner of an action.

senses.definition: One who is evicted.

core.definition: A person who has been forced to leave a home or property through a legal eviction order.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the last syllable, TEE, with light secondary stress on the first syllable. The vowel in ic is short, as in ik, not the long vowel of ike.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in legal and housing writing; sympathetic or critical in advocacy, depending on who is speaking.
nuance.usage_note: Evictee is a less common word used mainly in legal, housing and news writing. Americans more often say a person who was evicted, or a tenant who was evicted. The word describes someone who was removed by legal process, not someone who moved out voluntarily.

distinctions.note: A tenant is anyone who rents a property; an evictee is a tenant who has been removed by a legal eviction.
An evictee is the person forced out, while an evictor is the person or party who carries out the eviction.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is an evictee now, so she's staying with her sister.
examples.professional: The housing nonprofit tracks how many evictees return to shelter within six months.
examples.analytical: Researchers distinguish evictees from households that leave voluntarily, since legal removal has lasting effects on credit and employment.

nuance.analogy: An evictee is like a passenger removed from a flight by the crew: the removal was done to them, not chosen by them.
nuance.etymology: From evict plus -ee, a suffix meaning the person who undergoes the action.
common_mistakes: Using evictee for someone who moved out voluntarily.
Putting the stress on the first syllable instead of the last: ih-vik-TEE, not IH-vik-tee.

senses.definition: To the exclusion of anything or anyone else; solely or entirely.
senses.example: These new shoes are made exclusively out of recycled cardboard.

core.definition: Only; solely, with no one or nothing else included or involved.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the SKLOO syllable, the same as in exclusive. The final -ly is a quick lee, and the vowel in -sive stays short rather than becoming a long ee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it emphasizes a limit without judging it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exclusively in everyday talk and business writing to mean only: 'We sell exclusively online.' In speech, people often say only or just, which sounds more casual. Exclusively is a clear way to stress that nothing else is included.

distinctions.note: Only is simpler and more common in speech; exclusively is more formal and emphasizes that nothing else is included.
Solely is similar but more formal and often used for causes or responsibility, as in solely responsible.

examples.everyday: We've been eating takeout exclusively since the kids got sick.
examples.professional: Our reporting team works exclusively on the quarterly dashboard until the audit is finished.
examples.analytical: The argument rests exclusively on historical evidence, leaving the moral question entirely unexamined.

nuance.analogy: Like a radio tuned to a single station: it picks up that one signal and ignores all the others.
nuance.etymology: From exclusive plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using exclusively in casual speech where only or just would be more natural; it can sound stiff.
Stressing the wrong syllable: say ik-SKLOO-siv-lee, not ik-skloo-SIV-lee.

senses.definition: To clear of or to free from guilt; exonerate.
senses.example: The DNA evidence later exculpated the man, who had spent eleven years in prison.

core.definition: To prove or declare that someone is not guilty of a wrong or crime.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, EK-. The middle syllable is a reduced 'kul,' and the final 'pate' rhymes with 'mate.' Do not say 'ex-cul-PATE.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, because it describes clearing someone of blame.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exculpate mainly in legal, journalistic, and academic writing. In conversation people would say 'clear someone' or 'prove someone innocent.' It is used especially when evidence removes suspicion.

distinctions.note: Exonerate is the more common legal term and often implies an official finding. Exculpate can be used for any clearing of blame, formally or informally.
Acquit is a formal verdict in a trial. Exculpate describes the evidence or finding that clears someone.

examples.everyday: The security footage finally exculpated my brother, so the store dropped the accusation.
examples.professional: The audit logs exculpated the engineer, showing the error came from a faulty sensor.
examples.analytical: The historian argues that the newly found letters exculpate the minister from the charge of collusion.

nuance.analogy: To exculpate someone is like turning on a light that shows the shadow was never a person.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exculpare, 'to free from blame,' from ex- 'out' and culpa 'fault.'
common_mistakes: Confusing it with exculpatory, which is the adjective.
Stressing the last syllable as ex-cul-PATE.

exculpate.etymology: From Medieval Latin *exculpātus*, perfect passive participle of *exculpō* (see *-ate*), from *ex-* (“out, from”) + *culpa* (“fault; blame”) + *-ō*.

senses.definition: The ritual act of driving out evil spirits from persons, places or things that are possessed by them.

core.definition: A religious ritual of commanding evil spirits to leave a person, place, or object they are said to possess or afflict.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable: EK-sor-siz-um. The 'x' is /ks/, and the ending is a weak 'zum', not 'ISM' said fully.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; evokes fear or horror in pop culture, but is solemn and serious in church use.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often know the word from horror films like The Exorcist. In churches it is a formal rite, most associated with Catholic practice, and many Protestants speak of 'deliverance' instead. Use it seriously around believers.

distinctions.note: Deliverance is the usual term in Pentecostal and charismatic circles for freeing someone from demonic influence, often less formal than a rite of exorcism.
Possession is the condition of being controlled by a spirit; exorcism is the ritual response to it.
A blessing invokes God's favor and is routine; exorcism commands a spirit to leave and is rare and solemn.

examples.everyday: We watched The Exorcist last night, and I couldn't sleep after that exorcism scene.
examples.professional: In this seminar we will compare how Catholic and Pentecostal communities understand and practice exorcism.
examples.analytical: The Gospel accounts present exorcism not as magic but as a sign that God's kingdom is overpowering the forces of evil.

nuance.analogy: Like serving an eviction notice to an unwelcome tenant, but spoken in the name of God.
nuance.etymology: From Greek exorkizein, 'to bind by oath, adjure,' from ex- 'out' + horkos 'oath.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'ex-OR-sism' with the stress on the second syllable; stress the first: EK-sor-siz-um.
Confusing exorcism with 'exercise' because of similar sound.
Using 'exorcism' for ordinary cleansing rituals without any spirit element.
nuance.biblical_note: The Gospels often show Jesus casting out unclean spirits (Greek ekballo, 'to cast out', and exorkizo, 'to adjure'). Mark 1:21-28 shows Jesus teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum and silencing an unclean spirit with authority, amazing the crowd. Mark 5:1-20 tells of the man among the tombs whose demons Jesus sends into a herd of swine. Acts 19:13-16 describes itinerant Jewish exorcists who tried to use Jesus' name without faith and were overpowered.

traditions.view: Exorcism is a formal rite of the Church, carried out by a priest authorized by the bishop, following the Rite of Exorcism. A simple exorcism is also part of the baptismal liturgy.
Exorcism prayers, such as those of St. Basil, are part of baptism and are also used for the afflicted. They are understood as the Church's prayer for deliverance in Christ's name.

Views vary widely. Pentecostals and charismatics practice deliverance ministry. Many Reformed, Lutheran, and other traditions are cautious and stress prayer, pastoral care, and Christ's victory, with formal rites rare.

exorcism.etymology: From Old French *exorciser*, from Late Latin *exorcizō*, from Ancient Greek *ἐξορκίζω* (“to ward off, to charge under oath, adjure”), from *ἐξ* + *ὅρκος*.

senses.definition: A person, especially a priest or priestess, who is a practitioner in exorcism to force out evil spirits or demons from a living being.
