distinctions.note: Stir alone usually means mixing or moving a liquid or thing; stir up adds the idea of provoking strong feeling, trouble or a reaction.
Rile up is more informal and focuses on angering someone; stir up can mean either anger or enthusiasm.

examples.everyday: Don't stir up trouble at the party, just enjoy the food.
examples.professional: The new pricing plan stirred up a lot of questions from customers, so let's send out an FAQ.
examples.analytical: The author's essay stirred up debate about whether moral intuitions can justify philosophical claims.

nuance.analogy: Like a stick stirring up mud in a pond, the phrase brings hidden feelings or problems to the surface.
nuance.etymology: From the Old English styrian, to move, combined with up.
common_mistakes: Dropping up and saying stir a crowd when you mean excite a crowd, or using stir alone for trouble.
Adding the article in stir up the trouble; the common phrase is stir up trouble with no article.

senses.definition: A single pass of a needle in sewing; the loop or turn of the thread thus made.
senses.example: I cut myself badly while cooking and needed to go to hospital to get stitches.

senses.definition: An arrangement of stitches in sewing, or method of stitching in some particular way or style.
senses.example: cross stitch

senses.definition: An intense stabbing pain under the lower edge of the ribcage, brought on by exercise or laughing.
senses.example: I've got a stitch. I'm going to have to stop and rest.

senses.definition: A local sharp pain (anywhere); an acute pain, like the piercing of a needle.
senses.example: a stitch in the side

senses.definition: A single turn of the thread round a needle in knitting; a link, or loop, of yarn.
senses.example: drop a stitch

senses.definition: An arrangement of stitches in knitting, or method of knitting in some particular way or style.
A space of work taken up, or gone over, in a single pass of the needle.
A fastening, as of thread or wire, through the back of a book to connect the pages.
Any space passed over; distance.
Any least part of a fabric or clothing.
senses.example: to wet every stitch of clothes

senses.definition: An incorporation of an existing video into a new one, resulting in a collaborative clip that shows the two videos in a sequence.
A ridge of plowed land between two furrows.
A single pass of a surgical suture.
senses.example: I cut myself badly while cooking and needed to go to hospital to get stitches.

senses.definition: To form stitches in; especially, to sew in such a manner as to show on the surface a continuous line of stitches.
senses.example: to stitch a shirt bosom.

senses.definition: To sew, or unite or attach by stitches.
senses.example: to stitch printed sheets in making a book or a pamphlet.

senses.definition: To practice/practice stitching or needlework.
To form land into ridges.
To weld together through a series of connecting or overlapping spot welds.
To include, combine, or unite into a single whole.
senses.example: I can use this software to stitch together a panorama.

senses.definition: To combine two or more photographs of the same scene into a single image by putting them side by side and smoothing the edges.
senses.example: I can use this software to stitch together a panorama.

senses.definition: To incorporate (an existing video) into a new one, resulting in a collaborative clip that shows the two videos in a sequence.

core.definition: A single loop of thread made by one pass of a needle in sewing, knitting or embroidery.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is short, as in 'sit,' not the long 'ee' of 'sheet.' The ending 'tch' is a single sound, the same as in 'catch'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In idioms such as 'in stitches' the meaning is lighthearted, and 'a stitch in my side' is a plain complaint.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'stitch' in everyday talk about sewing, crafts and first aid, and it is the normal word for a single loop of thread. 'In stitches' means laughing very hard and is common in casual conversation. 'A stitch in my side' is the usual way to describe a sharp cramp while running.

distinctions.note: A seam is the line where two pieces of fabric are joined, while a stitch is one loop that makes up that line.
Sew is the general activity of making or repairing with needle and thread, while stitch focuses on the individual loops.

examples.everyday: I had to put a few stitches in the hem of my jeans before the trip.
examples.professional: The vendor's leather bag failed QA because the stitch density was too low at the seams.
examples.analytical: A stitch is a discrete unit, but a seam only has meaning as the pattern those units make together.

nuance.analogy: Like a single link in a chain: it looks small alone, but many links together hold the whole thing.
nuance.etymology: From Old English stice, 'a prick or puncture,' related to 'stick'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the vowel long, as in 'steet-ch'.
Saying 'in stitch' instead of 'in stitches' for laughing hard.

stitch.etymology: From Middle English *stiche*, from Old English *stiċe* (“a prick, puncture, stab, thrust with a pointed implement, pricking sensation, stitch, pain in the side, sting”), from **stiki*, from Proto-Germanic **stikiz* (“prick, piercing, stitch”), from…

senses.definition: A building for keeping goods of any kind, especially provisions.
A single location or resource where a large quantity of something can be found.
senses.example: This old book is a genuine storehouse of useful cooking tips.

senses.definition: To lay up in store.
senses.example: the mental storehousing of information

core.definition: A building or room where goods, supplies or provisions are kept for later use.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on STORE, with a secondary stress on HOUSE. The r is strongly pronounced, and HOUSE rhymes with 'mouse' rather than 'hose.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds slightly old-fashioned in everyday speech but is clear and precise.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use storehouse mainly in formal, literary or historical contexts, or to describe a large collection of information, such as 'a storehouse of knowledge.' In everyday speech they more often say warehouse, storage room or pantry. The verb sense, to lay up in store, is archaic.

distinctions.note: A warehouse is a large commercial building for storing goods for businesses, while a storehouse can be any place for keeping supplies, and is often used figuratively.
Storage is the general act or space of keeping things, while a storehouse is a specific building or resource.

examples.everyday: My grandfather called the old barn our family storehouse for tools and jars.
examples.professional: The data team described the warehouse as a storehouse of customer records, though it needed better governance.
examples.analytical: The library functions as a storehouse of tradition, preserving texts that might otherwise be lost to a community's memory.

nuance.analogy: A storehouse is like a pantry for an entire community: it holds what is needed until the season or need arrives.
nuance.etymology: Combines 'store' (Old French estore) with 'house' (Old English hus).
common_mistakes: Using 'storehouse' for a retail store, since it refers to a place for keeping goods.
Saying 'storehouse' with the stress on HOUSE instead of STORE.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Hebrew Bible the storehouse is often rendered from 'otsar (אוֹצָר), a treasury or storehouse where grain, wine, and treasure are kept. In Malachi 3:10 God tells the people to bring the full tithe into the storehouse so there will be food in his house, promising blessing in return. Genesis 41:56 describes Joseph opening the storehouses during the famine in Egypt to sell grain. Psalm 135:7 says God brings the wind out of his storehouses, picturing God as the keeper of creation's resources.

senses.definition: To become separated out into distinct layers or strata.
senses.example: Even without a pronounced social class system, people in a large society tend to stratify.

senses.definition: To separate out into distinct layers or strata.
senses.example: In this cut you can see how the sedimentary rock layers have been clearly stratified.

core.definition: To divide a population or dataset into separate subgroups, called strata, so that each subgroup can be analyzed on its own.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is a clear 'fy' with no reduction. Learners often say 'strah-TIF-y' or stress the second syllable, so keep the stress at the front.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: In American statistics and data science, you stratify a sample before drawing random samples within each group, for example stratifying survey respondents by age or region. In everyday talk, Americans say 'group' or 'sort' instead. The word also appears in sociology and geology, where it means forming layers or classes.

distinctions.note: Stratifying divides a population into groups that are each sampled, while cluster sampling randomly selects whole groups and samples within them.
Segment is a general business term for a market group, while stratify is a precise statistical method used to ensure each subgroup is represented.

examples.everyday: Before we run the survey, we should stratify the group by age so we don't end up with mostly young people.
examples.professional: Let's stratify the customer data by region and product line so the A/B test results are balanced across each segment.
examples.analytical: To stratify a population is to partition it into mutually exclusive subgroups whose internal variance is lower than the overall variance, which improves the precision of the estimate.

nuance.analogy: Like sorting a box of mixed cookies into separate trays by type before you count each tray.
nuance.etymology: From Latin stratum, 'layer', combined with -fy, 'to make'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable as 'strah-TIF-y'.
Using 'stratify' for simply sorting or ranking, when it means dividing into distinct layers or subgroups.

senses.definition: Miscellaneous items or objects; (with possessive) personal effects.
senses.example: What is all that stuff on your bedroom floor?He didn't want his pockets to bulge so he was walking around with all his stuff in his hands.

senses.definition: Unspecified things or matters.
senses.example: I had to do some stuff.

senses.definition: The tangible substance that goes into the makeup of a physical object.
senses.example: The stuff inside the mold hardened into a dense, glassy material within minutes.

senses.definition: Abstract/figurative substance or character.
senses.example: There is real stuff in her essay, with ideas that genuinely challenge conventional thinking.

senses.definition: Used as placeholder, usually for material of unknown type or name.
senses.example: Can I have some of that stuff on my ice-cream sundae?

senses.definition: Narcotic drugs, especially heroin.
senses.example: The dealer swore the stuff he sold was pure, but it nearly killed his customer.

senses.definition: Refuse or worthless matter; hence, also, foolish or irrational language.
senses.example: Don't give me any of that 'what-about' stuff!

senses.definition: Money.
senses.example: I'm short on stuff this month, so dinner out is off the table.

senses.definition: A melted mass of turpentine, tallow, etc. with which the masts, sides, and bottom of a ship are smeared for lubrication.
senses.example: The crew smeared the hull with melted stuff to keep seawater from seeping through the planks.

senses.definition: (dated) Pulp; paper stock ground ready for use. When partly ground, it is called half stuff.
senses.example: The mill ground the wood into stuff ready for paper, though the process took hours.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To fill by packing or crowding something into; to cram with something; to load to excess.
senses.example: I'm going to stuff this pillow with feathers.

senses.definition: To fill a space with (something) in a compressed manner.
senses.example: He stuffed his clothes into the closet and shut the door.

senses.definition: To fill with seasoning.
senses.example: She stuffed the turkey for Thanksgiving using her secret recipe.

senses.definition: To load goods into (a container) for transport.
senses.example: We stuffed the duffel bags with clothes, snacks, and a folded tent before leaving.

senses.definition: To sate.
senses.example: I’m stuffed after having eaten all that turkey, mashed potatoes and delicious stuffing.

senses.definition: To eat, especially in a hearty or greedy manner.
senses.example: She sits on the sofa all day, watching TV and stuffing herself with cream buns.

senses.definition: Used to contemptuously dismiss or reject something. See also stuff it.
senses.example: Stuff your stupid rules, I'll do what I like.

senses.definition: To heavily defeat or get the better of.
senses.example: Mudchester Rovers were stuffed 7–0 in the semi-final.

senses.definition: To cut off another competitor in a race by disturbing his projected and committed racing line (trajectory) by an abrupt maneuver.
senses.example: I got stuffed by that guy on the supermoto going into that turn, almost causing us to crash.

senses.definition: To preserve a dead bird or other animal by filling its skin.
senses.example: The museum hired an expert to stuff the bison that had stood in the hall since 1920.

senses.definition: To obstruct, as any of the organs; to affect with some obstruction in the organs of sense or respiration.
senses.example: Pollen season always stuffs my sinuses until I can barely breathe.

senses.definition: To form or fashion by packing with the necessary material.
senses.example: The tailor stuffed the cushion with wool, shaping it into a firm, round pillow.

senses.definition: To compress (a file or files) in the StuffIt format, to be unstuffed later.
senses.example: I stuffed the project files so the attachment would fit in the email.

senses.definition: (dated) To crowd with facts; to cram the mind of; sometimes, to crowd or fill with false or idle tales or fancies.
senses.example: Her grandfather had stuffed the children's heads with tales of ghosts and sea monsters.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: To eat a large amount of food until you are very full, often more than is comfortable or healthy.

pronunciation.tip: In everyday speech, one is reduced to a weak wun, and the main stress falls on self. In practice, you will say stuff yourself or stuffed myself more often than the full form.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative. It suggests overeating, usually in a joking or casual way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say I stuffed myself or I really stuffed myself, especially after a holiday meal or a buffet. It is informal and humorous. Say stuffed (adjective) to describe the feeling afterward: I'm so stuffed. A natural reply to someone offering more food is I'm stuffed, thanks.

distinctions.note: Overeat is neutral and general. Stuff oneself is more vivid and implies eating greedily or with great enthusiasm.
Gorge is more literary and suggests greedy, excessive eating. Stuff oneself is more casual.

examples.everyday: I really stuffed myself at the buffet, so I'm not hungry for dinner.
examples.professional: Don't stuff yourself at the team lunch, or you'll be sleepy for the afternoon review.
examples.analytical: Augustine's account of gluttony describes how people stuff themselves past need, and he treats the problem as a disorder of desire.

nuance.analogy: Stuffing oneself is like filling a suitcase past its zipper line: it holds more than it should, and it is uncomfortable to carry.
nuance.etymology: From stuff (verb), from Old French estoffer, to fill or furnish, with the reflexive oneself.
common_mistakes: Saying 'stuff myself' with stress on myself; the stress falls on self, as in mySELF.
Using stuff oneself in very formal writing, where overeat or gorge is more appropriate.

stuff-oneself.etymology: From Middle English *stuf*, *stuffe*, from Anglo-Latin *stuffa* and its etymon Old French *estofe*, *estoffe*, *estuf*, *estuffe*, *stoffe*, from *estoffer*, *estofer* (“to provide what is necessary, equip, stuff”), borrowed from Old High German *stoffōn*,…

senses.definition: Anything that is stunning.
senses.example: The sunset over the canyon was an absolute stunner, and we just stood there silently.

senses.definition: A woman or man of stunning beauty or handsomeness, a knockout.
senses.example: At the gala, the new lead actress was an absolute stunner in her emerald gown.

senses.definition: A professional wrestling maneuver in which an attacking wrestler applies a facelock to an opponent and falls to a seated position, forcing the opponent's jaw or neck to drop on the attacker's shoulder.
senses.example: The wrestler finished his opponent with a stunner, dropping him hard onto the mat.

senses.definition: A pistol firing a beam capable of stunning an enemy.
senses.example: In the sci-fi novel, the captain holstered his stunner after the intruders collapsed.

senses.definition: A person or machine that stuns an animal before slaughter.
senses.example: The slaughterhouse worker used a stunner on each animal before it reached the line.

core.definition: Someone or something extremely attractive or impressive, often in a surprising way.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The second syllable is a weak, r-colored er sound, not a separate oo, so the word has only two beats.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it is a compliment for appearance or for a striking result, though it can be used playfully.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stunner casually to praise someone's looks ('She's a real stunner') or to describe a surprising result ('The upset was a stunner'). It sounds warm and lively, so it suits friends, sports talk, and fashion comments. In formal writing, use striking or remarkable instead.

distinctions.note: Knockout is almost always about a person's beauty, while stunner can also describe a surprising result or an impressive object.
Showstopper refers to a performance or part of a show that earns applause; stunner is broader and more casual.

examples.everyday: Your new haircut is a stunner, and everyone at the party noticed.
examples.professional: The quarterly numbers were a stunner, so we need to find out what drove the growth before the board meets.
examples.analytical: Critics treated the film as a stunner, though its visual brilliance masks a thin argument about memory.

nuance.analogy: A stunner is like a bright floodlight in a dark room: it grabs attention before you can decide to look.
nuance.etymology: From stun with the suffix -er, meaning something or someone that stuns.
common_mistakes: Spelling it stunnor or stuner; the double n is required.
Confusing it with stunt man or stunt double, which refer to performers who do dangerous film scenes.

senses.definition: So as to stun or amaze.
senses.example: She was stunningly beautiful. I couldn't take my eyes off her.

core.definition: In a way that is extremely impressive, beautiful or surprising, used before an adjective or verb.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The final -ly is a clear lee sound, not lie, and the middle -ing is reduced to a short ih.

nuance.connotation: Positive in most uses: it intensifies praise. It can be negative when describing something shockingly bad, as in 'stunningly incompetent.'
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stunningly mostly before an adjective: 'stunningly beautiful,' 'stunningly simple,' 'stunningly good.' It sounds emphatic, so it works well in reviews, pitches, and enthusiastic talk. In casual speech people often choose really or incredibly, so stunningly can sound a little dramatic.

distinctions.note: Remarkably is milder and more neutral, suggesting something unusual; stunningly suggests a stronger, almost overwhelming impression.
Incredibly is a broad, everyday intensifier; stunningly carries a sense of visual or emotional impact.

examples.everyday: Her homemade lasagna was stunningly good, and she refused to give me the recipe.
examples.professional: The prototype is stunningly simple, so I think we can ship it without the extra middleware.
examples.analytical: The argument is stunningly simple, yet it hides a contested assumption about what counts as evidence.

nuance.analogy: Stunningly works like a dimmer switch turned all the way up: the normal level of the word suddenly becomes much brighter.
nuance.etymology: From stunning with the suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final -ly as lie; it is lee.
Using stunningly with a verb in ordinary speech where really or amazingly sounds more natural.

senses.definition: The transformation of an impulse into something socially constructive.
Elevation; exaltation; a making sublime.
senses.example: Her sermon on the sublimation of human desire toward God moved the whole congregation.

senses.definition: The transition of a substance from the solid phase directly to the vapor state such that it does not pass through the intermediate liquid phase.
senses.example: Dry ice undergoes sublimation at room temperature, turning straight from solid to gas.

core.definition: In psychology, the redirecting of an unacceptable impulse, such as anger or desire, into a socially acceptable activity, like sports or art.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on MAY, and the middle syllables are reduced to 'luh'. The final '-tion' sounds like 'shun', and non-native speakers often stress the first syllable instead.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive in ordinary psychology discussions, since it describes healthy coping, though Freudian theory is debated.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sublimation mainly in psychology, therapy, and chemistry classes. In everyday speech they usually say 'channeling' the emotion into something productive. The chemistry sense, where a solid turns straight into gas, is common in school science and industry.

distinctions.note: Repression pushes an impulse out of awareness, while sublimation transforms it into an acceptable outlet.
Displacement redirects feeling onto a less threatening target, while sublimation changes the impulse into a constructive activity.

examples.everyday: After his breakup, he channeled all that anger into training for marathons, which is a healthy kind of sublimation.
examples.professional: Our manager suggested the hackathon could be a sublimation of the team's frustration with the old pipeline into something productive.
examples.analytical: Freud treated sublimation as a mature defense in which sexual or aggressive energy is redirected into cultural achievements such as art or science.

nuance.analogy: Like a river diverted into a canal that turns a mill: the same energy is redirected into useful work.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sublimatio 'a lifting up', from sublimare; the chemical sense came into English first, and the psychological sense came from Freud's work.
common_mistakes: Using sublimation as a synonym for repression, when the two work in opposite ways.
Stressing the first syllable as in SUB-luh-may-shun.
Confusing the noun sublimation with the verb sublimate, which is used in the same way but with a different grammar.

sublimation.etymology: From Middle English *sublimacioun*, *sublimacion*, from Medieval Latin *sublīmātiō*, from Latin *sublīmō* (“to raise, to elevate”).

senses.definition: A stochastic process for which the conditional expectation of future values given the sequence of all prior values is superior or equal to its current value.
senses.example: If a gambler repeatedly plays a game with positive expectation, his payoff over time is a submartingale.

core.definition: A stochastic process whose expected future value, given all its past values, is greater than or equal to its current value.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on SUB, with secondary stress on mar and gale. Pronounce the r in mar clearly, as Americans do, and do not stress the final syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no evaluative meaning.
nuance.usage_note: This is a specialized term used in probability theory, mathematical finance and statistics courses. Americans use it in research papers, lectures and advanced data science work on time series and sequential decisions. You will rarely hear it outside those settings, so define it in one sentence when you explain it to non-specialists.

distinctions.note: A martingale has expected future value equal to its current value, while a submartingale has expected future value at least as large.
A supermartingale has expected future value at most its current value, which is the reverse inequality.

examples.professional: The loss process in our model behaves like a submartingale, so we can apply the convergence theorem to bound it.
examples.analytical: By the Doob decomposition, every submartingale splits uniquely into a martingale plus a predictable, nondecreasing process starting at zero.

nuance.analogy: A submartingale is like a stock that is expected to drift upward on average, while a martingale is like a fair coin game where you expect to break even.
nuance.etymology: From sub- (under, here meaning less than or equal to) plus martingale; the origin of martingale itself is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Confusing submartingale with supermartingale, which has the opposite inequality.
Stressing the final syllable (-GALE) instead of the first.

senses.definition: The process of making or classing (something or somebody) as subordinate.
senses.example: Her constant subordination of personal goals to team priorities frustrated the ambitious engineer.

senses.definition: The property of being subordinate; inferiority of rank or position.
The quality of being properly obedient to a superior (as a superior officer); this quality as a systemic principle of discipline within a hierarchical organization.

core.definition: The state of being placed in a lower rank or position, or of obeying the authority of someone above.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on NAY, the third syllable, with a weaker secondary stress on BOR. The -tion ending is 'shun', and the final syllable is a syllabic n, so it doesn't add an extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in management and theology. It can sound negative when it implies unfair control or lack of freedom.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use subordination in academic, legal, and organizational writing, and in theology when discussing relationships within the Trinity or within a hierarchy. In everyday talk people say 'being under someone' or 'taking orders'. The word is precise and can sound heavy in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Obedience is the act of following commands, while subordination is the broader condition of being structurally placed under another's authority.
Hierarchy is the whole system of ranks, while subordination describes a particular relationship within it.

examples.everyday: Kids often feel a sense of subordination at home, especially when they're the youngest.
examples.professional: Clear reporting lines reduce confusion about subordination and decision rights on the team.
examples.analytical: The subordination of the Son to the Father was debated fiercely in the fourth century.

nuance.analogy: Subordination is like the layers of a pyramid: each level rests on the one below, and each is under the authority of the one above.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin subordinatio, from subordinare 'to place under'.
common_mistakes: Using subordination for a single act of obeying, when obedience is usually better.
Pronouncing the final syllable with a full vowel, as 'nay-shun-ay'.

subordination.etymology: From Middle French *subordination*, from Medieval Latin *subordinatio*.

senses.definition: A coordinate space invoked in supersymmetry.

core.definition: In theoretical physics, an extended space whose added anticommuting coordinates encode supersymmetry.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SU. The second syllable is reduced, and the final -space rhymes with 'place' with a clear ay sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use superspace mainly in theoretical physics, string theory and advanced math courses. It is not a casual word and is not the same as hyperspace from science fiction. If someone asks what you study, you might explain it briefly, but most people outside physics will not know the term.

distinctions.note: Spacetime is the ordinary four-dimensional arena of relativity; superspace adds extra anticommuting coordinates to describe supersymmetry.
Hyperspace in popular culture usually means travel through an extra dimension; superspace is a precise mathematical construction used in physics.

examples.everyday: My nephew asked what superspace is, and I told him it's a math tool physicists use for a symmetry idea.
examples.professional: Our paper rewrites the action in superspace, which keeps the supersymmetry manifest through the calculation.
examples.analytical: Working in superspace makes the algebra of supersymmetry transformations easier to track, although the geometry becomes more abstract.

nuance.analogy: Superspace is like adding a hidden dimension of bookkeeping to a map, so every supersymmetry move is recorded in a single coordinate system.
nuance.etymology: From super- 'beyond' plus space; the prefix refers to the supersymmetric extension of ordinary spacetime.
common_mistakes: Confusing superspace with hyperspace from science fiction, which refers to fictional faster-than-light travel.
Treating superspace as a physical place rather than a mathematical construction.

senses.definition: A room or department where surgery is performed.
senses.example: The nurse guided us down the hallway to the surgery on the third floor.

senses.definition: A pre-packaged bankruptcy or "quick bankruptcy".
senses.example: Lawyers recommended a prepackaged surgery to clear the company's debts before summer.

senses.definition: The production of a manifold by removing parts of one manifold and replacing them with corresponding parts of others.
senses.example: Engineers used surgery to build a new manifold by swapping parts between two designs.

senses.definition: Drastic changes made to anything.
senses.example: The city council voted for surgery on the tax code, rewriting nearly every section.

senses.definition: The act or process of medical intervention involving incisions to remove, repair, or replace a part of a body; an instance of this process (a procedure).
senses.example: Surgery is often necessary to prevent cancer from spreading.

senses.definition: The medical specialty related to the performance of surgical procedures.
senses.example: She is training in surgery and hopes to specialize in cardiac procedures.

core.definition: Medical treatment in which a doctor cuts into the body to repair, remove, or replace a part of it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle syllable is a weak schwa, and the final syllable is 'ree,' not 'ger-ee,' so avoid over-pronouncing the g.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in general use but emotionally heavy, because it often involves fear, recovery, or serious illness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say have surgery or undergo surgery, not make surgery, and they often add the type, as in knee surgery. The room or department is also called surgery in hospitals, as in the surgery wing. In everyday talk, people say I'm having surgery on Monday rather than discussing the technical details.

distinctions.note: Operation is a common term for a surgical procedure, while surgery can also mean the medical field or the surgical department.
Procedure is broader and can be non-surgical, such as a blood test, while surgery requires cutting into the body.

examples.everyday: I had knee surgery last spring, and I'm finally walking without a limp.
examples.professional: The surgery was scheduled for seven, so we need to be at the hospital by six.
examples.analytical: Surgery raises ethical questions about consent and risk that medicine has only partly resolved.

nuance.analogy: Surgery is like a carefully planned renovation inside a sealed house, where every change must be made without collapsing the structure.
nuance.etymology: From Old French surgerie, from Latin chirurgia, from Greek kheirourgia, meaning hand-work.
common_mistakes: Saying make surgery instead of have surgery or undergo surgery.
Stressing the wrong syllable as sur-JER-ee; the stress is on the first syllable.

surgery.etymology: From Middle English *surgerie*, from Old French *surgerie*, from Latin *chirurgia*, from Ancient Greek *χειρουργία*, from *χείρ* (“hand”) + *ἔργον* (“work”).

senses.definition: Causing surprise.
senses.example: A surprising number of people attended the rally.

senses.definition: A situation in which somebody is surprised.
senses.example: The surprising of the guests at her party was planned for weeks in advance.

core.definition: Causing surprise because it is unexpected or unusual.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, PRY, and keep the first syllable weak. The ending '-ing' is short, like 'ih-ng', not a long 'eeng' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the word itself does not show whether the thing is good or bad. 'A surprising kindness' sounds positive, while 'a surprising mistake' sounds negative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'surprising' for facts, results and events, as in 'It's surprising how fast it snowed.' It is neutral and very common in both casual and professional speech. For a stronger reaction, people often say 'astonishing' or 'shocking'. In conversation, 'Not surprising!' is a common reply to bad news that you expected.

distinctions.note: 'Surprised' describes how a person feels, as in 'I was surprised', while 'surprising' describes the thing that causes the feeling, as in 'The news was surprising'.
'Unexpected' only says something did not happen as predicted, while 'surprising' adds that the thing is notable or striking.

examples.everyday: It's surprising how cheap the tacos are at that place on Fifth Street.
examples.professional: The surprising result is that the simpler model outperformed the deep network on the holdout data.
examples.analytical: It is surprising that a theory so confident about human freedom should rest on such a narrow account of desire.

nuance.analogy: A surprising result is like a familiar road that suddenly turns onto a path you had never seen.
nuance.etymology: From surprise (noun), with the present-participle suffix -ing used as an adjective.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I was surprising' when you mean 'I was surprised'; the adjective ending '-ed' describes the person's feeling.
Saying 'It's surprised that' instead of 'It's surprising that'.

senses.definition: An artistic movement and an aesthetic philosophy that aims for the liberation of the mind by emphasizing the critical and imaginative powers of the subconscious.
senses.example: Her early paintings were influenced by surrealism, with melting clocks and floating figures.

senses.definition: Art with a surreal aesthetic or narrative, regardless of whether or not it is linked to the surrealist movement.
senses.example: The film's dreamlike logic and strange imagery made it a piece of surrealism from start to finish.

core.definition: An early twentieth-century art and literary movement that uses dreamlike images and the unconscious mind.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on REE, the second syllable. The word has five syllables, and the final "-ism" is a weak, reduced ending, not a strong "ih" sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a respected cultural term and can be used with interest or criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use surrealism when discussing art history, film, literature or design. In casual talk, people might say that something is "very surreal" rather than naming the movement. When naming the movement, capitalize the Surrealist movement when you mean the historical group.

distinctions.note: Surreal is an adjective for a dreamlike feeling; surrealism is the noun for the movement or style.
Dada was an earlier, more anti-art movement; surrealism grew out of it with a focus on the unconscious.

examples.everyday: My daughter loves surrealism, so we went to the Dalí exhibit at the museum on Saturday.
examples.professional: Our design team borrowed surrealism for the ad campaign, using odd and dreamlike imagery to stand out.
examples.analytical: André Breton's 1924 manifesto defines surrealism as a revolt of the unconscious against rational constraint.

nuance.analogy: Surrealism is like a dream that has been painted or written down, with its logic turned sideways.
nuance.etymology: From French surréalisme, coined by Guillaume Apollinaire in 1917, from sur- ("above") and réalisme ("realism").
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in "SUR-ee-uh-liz-um".
Confusing surrealism with surreal; surrealism is the movement or style, surreal is the adjective for the feeling.

senses.definition: Of, or relating to the modernist art movement surrealism; having a similar surreal aesthetic or narrative.
senses.example: The gallery's exhibition featured surrealist paintings with melting clocks and dreamlike, impossible landscapes.

senses.definition: A surrealist artist.
senses.example: The surrealist showed her collection of dreamlike sculptures at a small gallery in Chicago.

core.definition: Relating to surrealism, the early twentieth-century art movement that used dreamlike, illogical images drawn from the unconscious.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, REE, and say the middle 'ea' as a quick 'ee-uh' glide. The ending '-ist' is short, like 'ist', not 'eest'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in art and literary criticism; it describes a deliberate style. In casual speech, it can sound strange or pretentious if used for ordinary oddness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'surrealist' mostly for art, film and literature, as in 'Dalí is the best-known surrealist painter.' In everyday speech people more often say 'surreal' to describe something bizarre, and 'surrealist' sounds more technical. Capitalize 'Surrealist' when you refer to the movement or its members.

distinctions.note: 'Surreal' is the everyday word for something bizarre and dreamlike, while 'surrealist' ties that quality to the specific art movement.
'Absurd' means ridiculous or illogical, usually with a negative tone, while surrealist work is deliberately strange and dreamlike.

examples.everyday: The dream was so surrealist that I woke up laughing at a talking giraffe.
examples.professional: The gallery's new show focuses on the surrealist painters of the 1920s and their influence on advertising.
examples.analytical: Her surrealist technique deliberately disrupts the viewer's expectation that a painting should tell one coherent story.

nuance.analogy: Surrealist art is like a dream painted on canvas: familiar objects placed in impossible relationships.
nuance.etymology: From French surréaliste, from sur- (beyond) and réaliste (realist).
common_mistakes: Using 'surrealist' as the name of the movement; the movement is 'surrealism' and the artist is a 'surrealist'.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'suh-ree-UH-list'; the main stress is on REE.

senses.definition: To maintain, or keep in existence.
senses.example: The professor had trouble sustaining students’ interest until the end of her lectures.

senses.definition: To provide for or nourish.
senses.example: provisions to sustain an army

senses.definition: To encourage or sanction (something). (The addition of quotations indicative of this usage is being sought:)
senses.example: The board refused to sustain any policy that quietly encouraged reckless spending.

senses.definition: To experience or suffer (an injury, etc.).
senses.example: The building sustained major damage in the earthquake.

senses.definition: To confirm, prove, or corroborate; to uphold.
senses.example: to sustain a charge, an accusation, or a proposition

senses.definition: To keep from falling; to bear; to uphold; to support.
senses.example: A foundation sustains the superstructure; an animal sustains a load; a rope sustains a weight.

senses.definition: To aid, comfort, or relieve; to vindicate.
senses.example: Her faith sustained her through the long months of chemotherapy and uncertainty.

senses.definition: To allow, accept, or admit (e.g. an objection or motion) as valid.
senses.example: The judge sustained the objection, and the jury was told to disregard the testimony.

senses.definition: To be a long-lasting sound.
senses.example: I like how long that drum sustains.

senses.definition: Clipping of sustainability.
senses.example: The sustain team at our company reports directly to the chief operating officer.

senses.definition: A mechanism which can be used to hold a note, as the right pedal on a piano.
senses.example: Press the sustain pedal on the piano and let the chord ring out.

core.definition: To keep something going or in existence over time, or to support someone physically or emotionally.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on STAYN, the second syllable. The vowel is a diphthong, so it sounds like 'stayn' rather than 'stan'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It implies keeping something good going, and it can mean holding up under pressure.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sustain in business and science to mean keeping a rate or effort going, and in everyday talk to mean support, as in 'sustain yourself'. It is more formal than 'keep up' or 'keep going'. For injuries, Americans say 'sustain an injury' and it is common in news.

distinctions.note: Maintain focuses on keeping something in good condition; sustain focuses on keeping it going over a long time, often under strain.
Support is general help; sustain is more about keeping something alive or going through difficulty.

examples.everyday: Eating a good breakfast helps me sustain my energy until lunch.
examples.professional: We need to sustain this level of performance through the next two quarters.
examples.analytical: A theory is only sustained if it can explain new evidence without collapsing into contradiction.

nuance.analogy: To sustain something is like keeping a fire alive: you keep adding fuel so the flame does not die.
nuance.etymology: From Old French sostenir, from Latin sustinere, to hold up or support.
common_mistakes: Confusing sustain with sustainable; sustain is a verb and sustainable is an adjective.
Using 'sustain' for a single short event instead of something that continues.

sustain.etymology: From Middle English *susteinen*, *sustenen*, from Old French *sustenir*, from Latin *sustineō* (“to uphold”), from *sub-* (“from below, up”) + *teneō* (“hold”).

senses.definition: Adventurous, exciting.

core.definition: Bold, adventurous, and dashing in a showy, sword-fighting way, like a romantic hero in an action movie.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on SWASH, with a lighter secondary stress on BUCK. Say the middle syllable clearly as 'buh' rather than dropping it, and keep 'ing' short.

nuance.connotation: Positive and admiring, with a playful, romantic flavor; it describes boldness and style rather than real danger.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use swashbuckling mostly for movies, novels, and characters, such as a swashbuckling pirate or a swashbuckling hero. It can also describe a bold, flashy business leader in a friendly or teasing way. It is rarely used for real violence, so do not use it for a serious crime.

distinctions.note: Daring means brave or willing to take risks; swashbuckling adds a flamboyant, romantic, almost theatrical style.
Dashing emphasizes charm and a stylish appearance; swashbuckling emphasizes adventurous action and bravado.
Swaggering often has a negative sense of arrogance; swashbuckling is usually admiring.

examples.everyday: My brother loves those old swashbuckling movies with sword fights on pirate ships.
examples.professional: Our new CEO has a swashbuckling style, so she launches products quickly and takes big bets.
examples.analytical: Early Hollywood's swashbuckling heroes embodied an idealized masculinity that the postwar era gradually questioned.

nuance.analogy: Like a movie hero leaping from ship to ship with a sword, the word describes boldness with a flourish.
nuance.etymology: From swash (to swagger or bluster) plus buckler (a small shield), originally for a boisterous, bullying swordsman in 16th-century England.
common_mistakes: Using it for quiet or cautious adventure; the word implies flashy, theatrical boldness.
Confusing it with buckle, the fastening device; the word comes from buckler, a shield.

swashbuckling.etymology: as though that had been formed as swashbuckle + -er.

senses.definition: A perennial wetland plant, Acorus calamus, with an aromatic medicinal root, formerly used to strew floors.

core.definition: A wetland plant with sword-shaped leaves and a spicy-smelling root, once used in folk medicine and to scent floors.

pronunciation.tip: Stress FLAG more strongly than sweet, which is lighter. Flag rhymes with bag, and the final g is a clear hard g, not a sound like flay.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a plant name used in botany, gardening, and herbal writing, with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Most Americans would not use this name in everyday talk unless they garden, forage, or study herbs. Gardeners and naturalists use it for wetland and pond plantings. Americans may also say calamus, the Latin name, in scientific or herbal contexts.

distinctions.note: Calamus is the scientific or Latin name for the same plant, used in botany. Sweet flag is the common English name that most Americans would use.
A cattail has a dense brown, sausage-shaped flower spike and flat leaves, while sweet flag has iris-like leaves and a greenish spadix.

examples.everyday: My neighbor dug up some sweet flag from the pond edge and said the root smells like ginger.
examples.professional: The restoration crew replanted sweet flag along the eroded creek bank to hold the soil in place.
examples.analytical: Early herbals praised sweet flag as a remedy, but its medicinal uses have largely been replaced by modern drugs.

nuance.analogy: Like a backyard herb that grows in the mud: fragrant, useful, and easy to overlook.
nuance.etymology: Sweet refers to its fragrant root, flag names iris-like marsh plants, and calamus comes from Greek kalamos, meaning reed.
common_mistakes: Assuming flag refers to the national flag; here it means an iris-like marsh plant.
Pronouncing flag with a long vowel as in flay instead of the short a in bag.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew qaneh bosem (קָנֶה בֹשֶׂם), meaning aromatic cane, is often identified with calamus, which is probably sweet flag or a related aromatic reed. It appears in Exodus 30:23 as an ingredient of the holy anointing oil, in Song of Songs 4:14 among the fragrant garden plants of the beloved, and in Jeremiah 6:20 as a costly import that God says does not please him. These passages show that the plant was valued as a rare, expensive fragrance.

senses.definition: A person who is much loved.
senses.example: Thanks for picking up the kids, sweetie; you're the best husband anyone could ask for.

senses.definition: A sweetheart.
senses.example: They met in college and she still calls him sweetie after thirty years of marriage.

senses.definition: A fruit that is a crossbreed between a grapefruit and a pomelo, originating in Israel.
senses.example: The grocer swore the sweetie in the crate was sweeter than any grapefruit.

core.definition: A term of affection for someone you love, such as a child or partner, or a very lovable person.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final -ie is an unstressed ee sound, like the y in happy, so say SWEE-tee and not SWEE-tih with a full vowel.

nuance.connotation: Warm and affectionate, but casual. It can sound patronizing when used with an adult you do not know well.
nuance.usage_note: Parents often say sweetie to children, and partners or close friends use it casually. In some parts of the South and Midwest, a server or clerk might say it warmly to customers, though this is less common in formal settings. As a fruit, a sweetie is a grapefruit-pomelo hybrid sold in American grocery stores.

distinctions.note: Sweetheart is warmer and more romantic, while sweetie is more casual and often used for children.
Honey and sweetie are both casual and common, but honey is used a bit more widely across ages and regions.
Sugar is a regional Southern term of affection, while sweetie is used more broadly across the country.

examples.everyday: Thanks for picking up the kids, sweetie.
examples.professional: She's a sweetie, but in the client meeting I'd keep the tone businesslike.
examples.analytical: Affectionate nicknames like sweetie can blur the line between intimacy and unequal power at work.

nuance.analogy: Like a soft blanket: warm and comfortable at home, but not what you would wear to a formal event.
nuance.etymology: A diminutive of sweet, formed with the suffix -ie or -y.
common_mistakes: Using sweetie with a stranger at a store or office, where it can sound patronizing.
Forgetting that the fruit called sweetie is a brand-style name that is usually capitalized as Sweetie.

senses.definition: Having a swinging motion.
Characteristic of swing music.
senses.example: The quartet played a swingy arrangement of the old standard, and the crowd started dancing immediately.

senses.definition: Having many swing voters.
senses.example: Analysts expect the suburban counties to stay swingy, deciding the state's close presidential race.

senses.definition: Allowing stones to curl more than usual.
senses.example: The ice was so swingy near the hog line that every stone drifted farther than the skip expected.

senses.definition: Variable in mood; liable to having mood swings.
senses.example: My teenage son has been so swingy lately, cheerful one minute and furious the next.

senses.definition: Inconsistent in performance.
senses.example: The rookie pitcher was swingy all season, brilliant one start and hopeless the next.

core.definition: Moving with a loose, swinging motion, such as a skirt or ponytail that sways as you walk.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final y is a long ee sound, so the word ends in a bright vowel. Don't add a g after the ng.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It usually describes something lively and loose, such as clothing or motion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use swingy casually in fashion talk, as in 'a swingy skirt', and in sports coverage of motion. The political sense, describing many swing voters, is uncommon; Americans usually say swing state or swing district instead.

distinctions.note: Swinging can describe lively nightlife or a fashionable scene; swingy describes physical motion of a loose object.
Flowing suggests smooth, continuous movement; swingy emphasizes the back-and-forth motion of something hanging loose.

examples.everyday: I love this dress; the swingy skirt moves so nicely when I walk.
examples.professional: Our sales numbers have been swingy this quarter, so I hesitate to forecast next month.
examples.analytical: Pundits describe a district as swingy when its results change sides from one election to the next.

nuance.analogy: Swingy is like a playground swing that never quite comes to rest at the same spot.
nuance.etymology: Formed from swing with the adjective suffix -y.
common_mistakes: Using swingy for a rhythm or style of music; for jazz music Americans say swing or swinging.
Writing 'swingey' with an extra e; the standard spelling is swingy.

senses.definition: The association of homologous maternal and paternal chromosomes during the initial part of meiosis.

core.definition: The pairing of homologous maternal and paternal chromosomes during the early stage of meiosis, the process that makes sex cells.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, NAP. The first and last syllables are reduced, so the word ends in a quick sis rather than a long ee sound. Learners often confuse it with synapse, which has the same stress but ends differently in the plural.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use synapsis almost only in biology, genetics and medical teaching, usually in textbooks, lectures or lab work. It is not used in everyday talk. When discussing neurons, Americans say synapse, so context is important.

distinctions.note: A synapse is a junction between nerve cells; synapsis is the pairing of chromosomes in meiosis. The two words share a root but describe unrelated processes.
Meiosis is the whole process of dividing cells to produce gametes, while synapsis is only one early stage within it.
Crossing over, the exchange of chromosome segments, happens after synapsis has brought the homologs together.

examples.everyday: My biology teacher kept saying the chromosomes need synapsis before they can swap pieces.
examples.professional: In the genetics lab, we confirm synapsis with fluorescent markers before we score the crossover frequency.
examples.analytical: Defects in synapsis during prophase I often lead to chromosome segregation errors and aneuploidy in gametes.

nuance.analogy: Like dancers finding their matching partners before the music changes, the homologous chromosomes pair up before they exchange pieces.
nuance.etymology: From Greek sunapsis, 'junction, connection,' from sunaptein, 'to join together.'
common_mistakes: Confusing synapsis (chromosome pairing) with synapse (nerve junction), which can make a biology answer sound wrong.
Stressing the wrong syllable, such as sih-NAP-sis with a long final vowel; the ending is short.

senses.definition: Of, related to or produced by a synod; synodal.
Of or pertaining to the conjunction of two or more heavenly bodies.
senses.example: a synodic month

core.definition: Relating to the period between two successive conjunctions of the same heavenly bodies, such as the synodic month.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, NAH, which has the open 'ah' vowel of 'cot' in General American. The first syllable is reduced to a short 'ih'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise scientific term with no emotional force.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in astronomy, and the phrase synodic month is the most common form. In ordinary conversation people say 'lunar month' or 'the cycle of the moon' instead. The ecclesiastical meaning of synod is less common in everyday American English and is usually written as synodal.

distinctions.note: Synodic measures time between repeated alignments as seen from Earth, while sidereal measures time relative to the fixed stars, so the two periods differ.
Synodic is mainly astronomical, while synodal relates to a church synod or assembly.

examples.everyday: My kid asked why the moon's shape changes, and I told her about the synodic month, the roughly 29.5-day cycle.
examples.professional: The mission planner used the synodic period of Mars to choose the best launch window.
examples.analytical: The ancient calendar was built on the synodic cycle of the moon rather than on the solar year.

nuance.analogy: A synodic period is like the time between two people in a race passing the same marker, not counting who is ahead of whom overall.
nuance.etymology: From Greek synodos 'meeting together', from syn- 'together' and hodos 'way'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, saying 'SIN-od-ik'.
Confusing synodic with synodal, which refers to church assemblies.

synodic.etymology: From Latin *synodicus*, from Ancient Greek *συνοδικός* (“of or related to an assembly or meeting”).

senses.definition: A term (word or phrase) which is synonymous with others.
senses.example: “Happy” is a synonym of “glad”.

senses.definition: Any of the various names that could in theory be used for a taxon in accordance with the relevant rules.
senses.example: Biologists must determine which name of the species is valid and which is a synonym under the code.

senses.definition: The subset of those names other than the one to be used according to the rules.
senses.example: The taxonomist listed three synonyms of the beetle in the appendix of the revision.

senses.definition: Any name that has been applied to a taxon other than the one to be used, including those not allowed by the rules such as misspellings or nomina nuda.
senses.example: The journal article catalogued every synonym, including misspellings and nomina nuda, for the genus.

senses.definition: An alternative (often shorter) name defined for an object in a database.
senses.example: Each product in the catalog can have a synonym that appears in search results.

senses.definition: To make synonymous.
senses.example: The data team decided to synonym the two customer IDs after the merge.

core.definition: A word or phrase that has the same or nearly the same meaning as another word or phrase in the same language.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SIN. The second syllable is a reduced 'uh' and the ending is a short 'nim', not 'nime'. Do not say 'sin-oh-NIM'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a neutral term used in everyday school and professional language.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say synonym in ordinary conversation, in school, and in writing, often when asking for another word. A thesaurus is the common tool for finding them. Use 'synonym for' or 'synonym of' followed by the word.

distinctions.note: An antonym has the opposite meaning, while a synonym has a similar meaning.
A homonym shares a spelling or pronunciation but has a different meaning, while a synonym shares meaning with a different word.
A paraphrase restates a whole sentence or passage in other words, while a synonym replaces a single word or phrase.

examples.everyday: Is 'big' a good synonym for 'large' when I describe a house?
examples.professional: Can you suggest a synonym for 'deliverable' that fits better in the status update?
examples.analytical: Some philosophers argue that no two words are perfect synonyms because context always adds some nuance.

nuance.analogy: A synonym is like a second name for the same person: different label, same person underneath.
nuance.etymology: From Greek synonymos 'having the same name', from syn- 'same' and onyma 'name'.
common_mistakes: Using 'synonym to' instead of 'synonym for' or 'synonym of'.
Stressing the second syllable, saying 'sih-NON-im'.

synonym.etymology: From Middle English *sinonyme*, from Latin *synōnymum*, from Ancient Greek *συνώνυμον*, neuter singular form of *συνώνυμος* (“synonymous”), from *σύν* (“with”) + *ὄνομα* (“name”).

senses.definition: Of or relating to a synopsis.
senses.example: The team prepared a synoptic report summarizing the quarter's findings for the board.

senses.definition: Obtained simultaneously over a wide area, for presenting a comprehensive and nearly instantaneous picture of the state of the atmosphere.
senses.example: The synoptic weather chart showed pressure systems across the entire Midwest at once.

senses.definition: Pertaining to the gospels of Matthew, Mark and Luke.
senses.example: In seminary, we compared the synoptic Gospels to see how Matthew, Mark, and Luke differ.

core.definition: Giving a general overview of a whole subject in a brief, comprehensive form, showing its main features together.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, NAP. The first and last syllables are reduced, so say 'sih-NAP-tik'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is an academic and technical adjective that sounds precise.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use synoptic mainly in academic, scientific, and religious writing. Its everyday meaning is close to 'overview' or 'big-picture,' so in conversation people often just say 'a big-picture view.' In biblical studies it has a separate, specific sense explained below.

distinctions.note: Comprehensive means complete in detail; synoptic means presenting a general overview that shows the whole at a glance.
Summary is a general word for a restatement; synoptic is a more formal adjective emphasizing a whole-view perspective.

examples.everyday: My sister gave me a synoptic view of the family history, just the big events.
examples.professional: The dashboard offers a synoptic view of all our services, so managers can spot outages quickly.
examples.analytical: Her synoptic account of the debate gives the main positions without losing their internal logic.

nuance.analogy: Like a city map seen from a plane, showing the whole layout rather than every street.
nuance.etymology: From Greek synoptikos, seeing together, from synopsis, a general view.
common_mistakes: Confusing synoptic with synoptical, which means the same but is less common in American writing.
Stressing the first syllable as SIN-op-tic.
nuance.biblical_note: In biblical studies, synoptic refers to the Gospels of Matthew, Mark and Luke, which can be read side by side because they share much material and order. Matthew 4:12-17 and Mark 1:14-15 both describe Jesus beginning his ministry in Galilee after John's arrest, a parallel that shows this closeness. Luke 1:1-4 states that many had compiled accounts, and Luke writes an orderly account, which helps readers see his method of gathering sources.

synoptic.etymology: From New Latin *synopticus*, from Ancient Greek *συνοπτικός* (“seeing the whole together or at a glance”), from *σύνοψις* (“a general view, synopsis”), from *συν-* (“with”) + *ὄψις* (“view”).

senses.definition: Having a flat (planar) horizontal surface at top.
senses.example: Mesas got their name from being tabular.

senses.definition: Organized as a table or list.
senses.example: In technical communication, don't use prose to present information that lends itself to a tabular presentation.

senses.definition: Calculated by means of a table.
senses.example: tabular artillery direction

senses.definition: Tending to split into thin flat pieces, as slate does.
senses.example: The local bedrock is tabular.

senses.definition: Tabular bone.

core.definition: Arranged in rows and columns like a table, or describing data stored in a structured grid.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TAB. The final syllable is a weak schwa with an American r, so say 'ler' with the r sound, not 'lar' with a strong vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is precise and descriptive.
nuance.usage_note: In American data work, tabular data means information organized in rows and columns, such as a spreadsheet or database table. It contrasts with unstructured data like images, audio or free text. In geology, tabular describes flat, sheet-like rock layers. Americans use it mainly in technical and academic contexts.

distinctions.note: Tabular is an adjective describing a form; tabulate is a verb meaning to arrange data into that form.
Columnar emphasizes columns; tabular covers the whole grid of rows and columns.

examples.everyday: The schedule came as a tabular list, so I could see every bus at a glance.
examples.professional: We store customer records as tabular data, with one row per transaction and one column per field.
examples.analytical: Tabular forms of knowledge, like the periodic table, reduce complex relations to a grid that reveals patterns.

nuance.analogy: Tabular data is like a well-kept ledger: each row is one record and each column is one field.
nuance.etymology: From Latin tabularis, relating to tables or boards, from tabula.
common_mistakes: Using tabular as a verb; the verb is tabulate.
Saying 'TAB-yoo-lar' with a strong final vowel instead of the reduced American -er ending.

senses.definition: To be cautious, careful or prudent.
senses.example: Take care when you’re crossing the crosswalk.

senses.definition: To mind, or be in charge of something.
senses.example: Could you take care of the dog while we're in Denver next week?

senses.definition: Good-bye (literally, take care of yourself)
senses.example: It was good seeing you, Ruth. Take care, and call when you get home.

core.definition: To be careful, or to look after yourself or something; in speech, used as a friendly goodbye.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KAIR, with a strong American r. The phrase is often reduced to 'tay-KAIR' in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Positive
nuance.usage_note: As a goodbye, 'Take care' is very common in American phone calls, emails and conversations with friends, family and colleagues. The usual reply is 'You too' or simply 'Bye.' For instructions, 'take care of' means be responsible for, and 'take care' alone can mean be careful.

distinctions.note: 'Be careful' warns about danger; 'take care' as a goodbye is affectionate, not a warning.
'Bye' is short and neutral; 'take care' adds warmth and concern for the other person's well-being.

examples.everyday: Thanks for dinner, Maria, take care and tell Carlos I said hi.
examples.professional: Thanks for the update on the project, I'll follow up Monday, take care.
examples.analytical: In Pauline usage, care is a moral and communal responsibility, and 'take care' echoes that obligation in ordinary speech.

nuance.analogy: It is a small wish folded into a goodbye, like handing someone an umbrella as they leave.
common_mistakes: Saying 'take care you' instead of 'take care of yourself'.
Using 'take care' for a warning in a dangerous situation; say 'be careful' there.

conversation.text: It was great to see you. Take care!
"Take care, Priya." "You too. Say hi to your mom."
Take care of yourself and get some rest.
Don't worry about the bill; I'll take care of it.

senses.definition: To start working at an official appointment to some office.

core.definition: To begin serving in an official government, political, or organizational position, usually after an election or appointment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on AW in 'office,' and the second syllable is a reduced vowel, so it sounds like 'AW-fis,' not 'AW-fees.' Americans with the cot-caught merger pronounce the first vowel the same as 'ah.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It sounds formal and ceremonial, marking the start of official responsibility.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in news, politics, and organizational reports, such as 'She will take office in January.' For the ceremony, people say 'be sworn in,' and for the formal oath they say 'take the oath of office.' In everyday talk, people say 'start the job' for ordinary work, since 'take office' is for official posts.

distinctions.note: Be sworn in describes the public ceremony, while take office describes the start of the official role.
Assume office is a very similar formal phrase, though take office is more common in American news.
Start a job is ordinary workplace language, while take office is reserved for official or elected positions.

examples.everyday: My cousin is taking office as the town clerk next month, so we're throwing a little party for her.
examples.professional: The new board members take office on July 1, so the transition committee has to finish the handover by June.
examples.analytical: Constitutional theorists debate whether a leader who takes office through a contested election has the same legitimacy as one who wins by a wide margin.

nuance.analogy: Like a driver taking the wheel at a shift change, the official begins formal responsibility at a set moment.
nuance.etymology: 'Office' comes from Latin officium 'duty, service, function.'
common_mistakes: Adding 'the' and saying 'take the office' when American English usually says 'take office.'
Confusing 'take office' with 'go to the office,' which means going to a workplace building.

senses.definition: Infatuated; fond of or attracted to.
senses.example: He was very taken with the girl, I hear.

senses.definition: In a serious romantic relationship.
senses.example: I can't ask her out, she's taken.

core.definition: Already in a committed romantic relationship and not available to date; sometimes also infatuated with or strongly attracted to someone.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, TAY. The final syllable is a syllabic n, so it has no separate vowel and sounds like 'kn' with a light 'uh' at most.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a friendly, lighthearted way to say you are in a relationship, and it can signal that you are not interested in someone's flirting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'I'm taken' jokingly when someone compliments them or flirts, and it usually ends the flirtation politely. The phrase 'taken with' means fond of or impressed by something, as in 'I'm taken with this idea.' Do not use 'taken' to describe your own interest in a person; say 'I'm into her' or 'I like him' instead.

distinctions.note: 'Single' describes someone not in a relationship in general; 'taken' specifically means the person is already committed to someone else.
'Taken with' means fond of or attracted to something or someone, without implying a relationship status.

examples.everyday: Thanks for the compliment, but I'm taken, so you're safe to talk to my friend Mike instead.
examples.professional: The sales team is completely taken with the new dashboard, so we should schedule the rollout for next month.
examples.analytical: Many readers are taken with Augustine's account of desire, yet they often overlook how he defines the will as the root of sin.

nuance.analogy: Like a library book with someone's name on the checkout slip: it is still on the shelf, but it is already checked out.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of take, from Old Norse taka, 'to grasp'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I am taking' to mean I am in a relationship; the correct word is 'taken'.
Using 'taken by' for your own feelings, as in 'I am taken by her'; say 'I'm taken with her' or 'I like her'.

taken.etymology: From Middle English *taken*, *takenn*, from Old English *tacen*, **ġetacen*, from Old Norse *tekinn*, from Proto-Germanic **tēkanaz*, past participle of Proto-Germanic **tēkaną* (“to take; grasp; touch”).

senses.definition: Mixed up, interlaced.
senses.example: tangled knot

senses.definition: Intricate.
senses.example: The tangled plot of the detective novel kept me guessing until the final chapter.

core.definition: Twisted together into a knotted mess, or so complicated and confused that it is hard to sort out.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the vowel is short a, as in 'bat'. The -ed ending is simply a d sound after the l, so the word has two syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it suggests confusion or difficulty, but can be used playfully for hair or messy plans.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tangled for hair, wires, plans, relationships, and stories: 'a tangled history' or 'a tangled web' for a complicated situation. In casual talk, 'my hair is so tangled' is very common. When you mean involved in something, use 'tangled up in' or 'tangled with', not 'tangled to'.

distinctions.note: Complicated is neutral about how hard something is; tangled suggests things are knotted together and hard to separate.
Messy describes disorder in general; tangled specifically describes things twisted or interlaced with each other.

examples.everyday: My hair is so tangled after the swim that I need a wide comb.
examples.professional: The budget and the marketing plan are so tangled that no one knows which numbers are final.
examples.analytical: The author traces a tangled history of colonial trade and religious reform, showing how each depended on the other.

nuance.analogy: Like a drawer of old charging cables, where every cord has wrapped itself around another.
nuance.etymology: Past participle form of tangle, from Middle English tangle, of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a long a (TAYNG-guld); the vowel is short.
Confusing tangled with tangled up in: the phrase 'tangled up in the situation' needs the preposition.

senses.definition: Clipping of tarpaulin (“covering”).
senses.example: We kept a spare tarp in the truck in case it rained on the lumber.

senses.definition: To cover something with a tarpaulin.
senses.example: Before the storm hit, we tarped the woodpile and secured the loose patio furniture.

core.definition: A large, heavy, waterproof sheet, usually plastic or canvas, used to cover things against rain, dust, or dirt.

pronunciation.tip: Keep the r clearly and use a long 'ar' vowel; the p at the end is unreleased, so the word ends quietly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a practical, everyday object.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tarp constantly for covering firewood, boats, trucks, roofs, and job sites. It is a clipped form of tarpaulin, which people use in more formal or technical contexts. As a verb, tarp is common in home and construction talk, as in 'I tarped the woodpile.'

distinctions.note: Tarpaulin is the full and more formal or technical word, often used in catalogs and manuals; tarp is the everyday short form.
A drop cloth is a thin cloth used to protect floors and furniture during painting, while a tarp is heavier and used outdoors.

examples.everyday: Throw a tarp over the firewood before the rain starts.
examples.professional: The crew tarped the exposed roof deck before the storm reached the job site.
examples.analytical: A tarp keeps material dry, but if it is sealed too tightly it traps condensation underneath.

nuance.analogy: Like a raincoat for your stuff: it keeps the weather off without changing what it protects.
nuance.etymology: Short for tarpaulin, from tar plus palling, a covering cloth.
common_mistakes: Saying 'tarp over' the object without necessity; 'tarp the woodpile' is equally natural.
Confusing tarp with tarpaulin in formal writing, where tarpaulin is more typical.

senses.definition: A person who studies or practises technology; an expert in a particular technology.
senses.example: The lift technician found the reason the lift wasn't working.

core.definition: A skilled worker who installs, maintains, or repairs equipment or performs hands-on technical work.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, NISH. The 'ti' is pronounced 'sh,' not 't' or 'tee,' and the final syllable is a soft 'un.' Do not say 'tek-NEE-shun.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It names a valued skilled job, though some people use it to mean someone who does not design the system.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, a 'technician' is a hands-on specialist: an IT technician, a lab technician, or a service technician who fixes equipment. Do not call a technician an 'engineer' if they do not design systems, since this can be a sensitive title distinction. People often say 'the tech' in casual talk for the same person.

distinctions.note: An engineer usually designs and analyzes systems and needs a formal degree, while a technician performs and maintains the work under the design.
A 'technologist' in American usage is often a trained specialist in a medical or lab field, such as a radiologic technologist, and is similar to a technician but with more formal training.

examples.everyday: The Verizon technician came out this morning and finally fixed the internet in our living room.
examples.professional: Ask the lab technician to recalibrate the sensor before the test so the readings are reliable.
examples.analytical: A technician's knowledge is often tacit, learned through practice rather than stated in formal theory.

nuance.analogy: A technician is like a skilled pilot who keeps the plane flying, while the engineer is the one who drew the blueprint.
nuance.etymology: From 'technic' (art or skill) plus the suffix '-ian,' meaning a person who practices or is skilled in something.
common_mistakes: Calling any computer worker a 'technician' when they design systems; use 'engineer' or 'developer' for design roles.
Mispronouncing 'ti' as 't' or 'tee'; it is pronounced 'sh.'

senses.definition: A person who completely abstains from alcoholic beverages.

core.definition: A person who completely abstains from alcoholic beverages and never drinks them.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, TEE. The last two syllables are reduced, so the word ends in a soft 'lur' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most contexts, though it can sound mildly teasing or judgmental, depending on who says it.
nuance.usage_note: Teetotaler is the standard American spelling and noun, used in everyday conversation and in writing. Americans often use it to describe themselves ('I'm a teetotaler') or in phrases like 'a lifelong teetotaler'. It can sound a little playful or old-fashioned, so use it with some care in serious contexts. A more neutral alternative is 'nondrinker'.

distinctions.note: Nondrinker is neutral and purely descriptive, while teetotaler suggests a firm, lifelong commitment to abstinence.
Abstainer is more formal and often appears in medical or legal writing, while teetotaler is common in everyday speech.

examples.everyday: My uncle is a teetotaler, so he orders iced tea at every barbecue.
examples.professional: When we plan the client dinner, we should remember that two of our guests are teetotalers.
examples.analytical: The social history of the teetotaler reveals how personal abstinence became a public marker of moral respectability.

nuance.analogy: A teetotaler is like a clean, dry cup at a party where everyone else is pouring wine.
nuance.etymology: From teetotal, the adjective, with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Spelling it teetotaller, the British form, in American writing.
Using teetotaler as an adjective; it is a noun, and the adjective is teetotal.

senses.definition: The act of temporizing.
The application of a temporary piece of dental work that will later be removed.

core.definition: The act of delaying a decision or action in order to gain time or avoid commitment.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on ZAY, the fourth syllable, with a lighter stress on TEM at the start. Keep the middle syllables quick and reduced, and do not stress the -iz- syllable.

nuance.connotation: Usually negative; it suggests stalling or evasion rather than sensible waiting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in political commentary, history, writing and formal discussion. Calling someone's stalling temporization implies they are avoiding a commitment. In dentistry it also names a temporary restoration, a technical sense that most people never meet.

distinctions.note: Procrastination is delay out of habit or avoidance; temporization is deliberate delay to gain time or advantage.
A compromise is an agreement reached by giving something up; temporization avoids making any choice at all.

examples.everyday: My landlord's temporization about the repairs is getting old; he keeps saying next week.
examples.professional: The team's temporization on the vendor decision has pushed the launch back two sprints.
examples.analytical: Historians often read the diplomacy of the 1930s as temporization, in which delay became a substitute for policy.

nuance.analogy: Like a traffic light that stays yellow: it avoids a decision but does not move anyone forward.
nuance.etymology: From temporize, from Latin temporizare, to wait for the right time, from tempus, time.
common_mistakes: Treating it as a positive word; it usually suggests stalling.
Confusing it with temporal or temporary, which are different in meaning.
